lawyer:
AJ Mohammad Ali, Senior Advocate, instructed by SM Rahman, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioners.
Md Fazlul Karim, Senior Advocate instructed by Md Nawab Ali advocate-on-Record ------ For Respondent No.1.
Not represented ------ For Respondent Nos.2.
parties:
Mustaque Hossain (Md)  ------ Petitioner 
Vs. 
Md Shajahan Miah and another  ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 26th April 2004 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision NO.305 of 2003 with Civil Revision NO.947 of 2003).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: The petitioner seeks leave to appeal against the judgment and order dated 26-4-2004 of the High Court Division making the Rules the Rule in Civil Revision No.305 of 2003 heard analogously with Civil Revision No.974 of 2003 absolute setting aside those dated 14-11-2003 allowing the Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 2003 of the Assistant Judge, 3rd Court Dhaka and setting aside the ex parte decree in see Suit No.3 of 393 and restoring the suit to its original file and number.

2. The respondent No.1 filed the SSC suit No.3 of 1993 in the Court of Assistant Judge Dhaka for eviction of the petitioner stating, inter alia, that he requires the suit shop for the purpose of giving accommodation to his son to start a business over there and he is the eldest son in his family and though matriculate but is unemployed and served notice on the defendants under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act to vacate the suit shop. That it appears that summons were regularly served on the defendant No.2 in the aforesaid suit; that it appears that the notices were also sent through registered post and acknowledgement of the same was duly received back by the Court.

3. The performa-respondent No.2 Md Abdul Hye contested the suit filling written statement stating, inter alia that no summon or notice was served upon him and that the defendant-petitioner purchased possession of 2 (two) shop rooms on payment of Taka 3,00,000 as possession value and 2 (two) separate lease deeds were executed by the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 in favour of the defendant petitioner and defendant-opposite party No.2 on 19-3-1981 and the rent was fixed at Taka 200 each i.e. equal to Taka 400 in total. Thereafter though the two shop rooms were converted into one room giving some portion of the suit shop room to the plaintiff and a new lease deed was executed on 13-4-1988 but the defendant petitioner and the defendant respondent No.2 have been running their business separately in keeping their separate goods in the shop rooms showing defendant respondent No.2's business in V Belt and defendant petitioner is running Hardware business by investing huge capital in the shop room separately. That the plaintiff No.1 in his own interest did not mention that the possession was transferred on account of Taka 3,00,000 in the lease deed but DWs 2 Abdul Motin in his deposition proved that the defendants paid Taka 3,00,000 to the plaintiff as possession value of the suit shops. It appears from the condition Nos.1 and 6 of the lease deed dated 13-4-1988 that after the death of the defendants their heirs shall inherit the tenanted premises and process continuously. The defendants were also given right to sell the possession of the suit shop rooms to the third party and third party shall enjoy all privileges from the plaintiff according to the lease deed of the defendant. It is also mentioned in the said lease deed that in case of transfer, of the suit shop rooms to the third party, the defendants would pay 10% (ten percent) upon total money to the plaintiff as the possession value which, amount shall be accepted by the defendants from the third party From the above conditions of the lease deed it is clear that the defendants purchased the possession of the suit shop room on payment of Taka 3,00,000.

4. The learned SCC Judge decreed the suit on contest against the defendant No.1 and ex parte against defendant No.2 petitioner by judgment and decree dated 17-11-1999. The defendant No.2 after collecting the information slip though his learned Advocate Mr Md Imtiaz Hossain on 27-11-1997 filed the Miscellaneous Case No.85 of 1997 in the 2nd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which was renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 2002 on transfer to the 3rd Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka for setting aside the aforesaid ex parte decree.

5. The plaintiff contested the Miscellaneous Case the same by filing written objection and upon an application dated 25-11-2001 filed by the defendant petitioner, the learned 2nd Court of Assistant Judge was pleased to stay all further proceedings of the Execution Case No. 2 of 2002 till disposal of the Miscellaneous Case No.85 of 1997, renumbered as Miscellaneous Case No. 6 of 2002 of the Court of 3rd Assistant Judge, Dhaka.

6. The learned Assistant Judge allowed the Miscellaneous Case setting aside the judgment and decree dated 17-11-97 in SCC Suit No.3 of 1993.

7. The plaintiff preferred Civil Revision No.305 of 2003 before the High Court Division and the Rule was made absolute.

8. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submits that having regard to the fact that the restoration of the SCC Suit No.3 of 1997 setting aside the ex parte decree through Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 2003 has been passed to give the petitioner an opportunity to defend himself in the case and, as such, the High Court Division failed to appreciate the same and most illegally made the rule absolute. The learned Counsel further submitted that having regard to the petitioner purchase of the possession of the premises on payment of salami and continuing with his tenancy right independently and the ex parte decree against him has been set aside by the trial Court and the same has been reversed by the High Court Division and the same being a case of reversal, the petitioner has a substantial cause for hearing in the appeal and, as such, his right to continue in the tenancy needs to be protected in the interest of justice.

9. In support of his submission the learned Counsel has referred to the decision in the case of Munshi Amiruddin Ahmed vs Begum Shamsun Nahar reported in 48 DLR 21 and submitted that though the tenant failed to pay rent within due date and became technically a defaulter, the receipt of salami of Taka 3,00,000 on the basis of established practice in the commercial world between the parties could be taken notice of by the Court, in order to operate the principle of promissory estoppel debarring the landlord to evict the petitioner from the tenanted premises, as a right independent of the tenancy right has accrued and created by the mutual consent between the parties.

10. Section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance prohibited the practice of receiving salami on condition of making the monthly tenancy transferable and non-ejectable as illegal. Clause (a) of section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance prohibits the acceptance of any sum of money over and above the rent payable by a tenant. The said clause has also made illegal even any claim or invitation of an offer for the payment of such sum of money in the form of premium, salami or fine either when a tenancy is being created or renewed or during its continuance. Under clause (b) no one is allowed to claim or receive a payment of more than one months rent, in advance. Such agreement for lease was void under section 23 of the Contract Act as its object was not lawful and that it having not been registered was unenforceable and also inadmissible in evidence.

11. The referred decision is sought to innovate a type of lease in which the tenant will not be ejectable for accepting the salamy. Such form of lease is not germane to the concept and proposition as to lease recognised under the law. A lease of immovable property is a transfer of a right to enjoy such property, made for certain time, express or implied, or in perpetuity, in consideration of a price paid or promised, or of money, a share of crops, service or any other thing of value, to be rendered periodically or on specified occasions to the transferor by the transferee, who accepts the transfer on such terms. The said definition of the lease has been provided under section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act. Apart from the above, no other form of lease sought to be innovated in the said decision has been contemplated under the law. Thus essential features constituting a lease are that the right must be one as to immovable property, the right must be that of enjoyment of immovable property, there must be a transfer of such right, the right of transfer is an interest in property, the transfer must be made for certain time, express of implied, or in perpetuity, the transfer must be one for consideration, the consideration must be of the particular kind namely, premium or rent, as defined by section either or both of them, but the consideration must be a legal one recognised by the concerned law on the subject.

12. Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act provides that the duration, of certain leases in absence of written contract or local usage, i.e., the lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by six months notice expiring with the end of a year of the tenancy, and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose shall be deemed to be a lease from month to month, terminable, on the part of either lessor or lessee, by fifteen days notice expiring with the end of a month of the tenancy.

13. Apart from the above, no other lease has been contemplated under the law and, as such, neither the Premises Rent Control Ordinance nor the Contract Act or the Transfer of Property Act contemplated any other lease, apart from those specified therein. Even any agreement between the parties could not operate as promissory estoppel to go beyond the provision of law which shall be deemed to be void.

<u>14. Section 10 of the Premises Rent Control Act, 1991 makes the illegal practice of payment of salami prohibited and that the tenant is entitled to refund of the salami paid by him within 6 months of such payment under section 14 and the landlord was liable to pay fine for receiving salami under section 3 of the said Act. The widespread and long standing practice of voluntary payment of salami in the commercial world did not make the tenant a non-ejectable one and no interest other than the tenancy right recognised by law could be created on payment of salami so as to prevent the tenant not liable to be ejected on specific legal ground for the purpose. Under section 18 of the Premises Rent Control Act the landlord is entitled to eject a tenant as soon as a monthly tenant is a defaulter or a landlord bonafide requires the premises or for building and rebuilding purpose.</u>

<u>15. In view of the above, the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioner are of no substance for the reasons aforesaid and being contrary to the provisions of law and the decision referred to above is not a sound proposition of law and could not be relied upon.</u>

<u>16. In that view of the matter, no question of any promissory estoppel arises on ground of acceptance of any, salami, for making a tenant non-electable, for such practice is not only prohibited by the said Act, but no right recognised by law could be attributed for acceptance of the salami to render the tenant non-electable in accordance with law.</u>

The petitions are dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Fazlul Karim with A Wahab, Advocates ----- For the Opposite-Party Nos.1-4.
parties:
Hamed Ali Chowdhury ------ Petitioner
vs. 
Nasir Mohammad Khan & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Hoque J: This Rule was issued directing the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the impugned order No. 149 dated 21.9.89, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 57 of 1978, so far it relates to continuation of the Suit against the present petitioner, (defendant No.1 (a) should not be set aside.

2. The facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are that the opposition parties as plaintiffs instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 57 of 1978 in the 3rd Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against Sayed Salamat Ali as defendant for specific performance of contract. It was alleged, as the defendant failed to execute and register a deed of sale, the plaintiffs had to institute the present suit for specific performance of contract. Later on, the present petitioner Hamid Ali Chowdhury was added as defendant No. 1 (a) in the suit at the instance of the plaintiffs. During hearing of the suit the plaintiffs examined 7 witnesses. When the defendant No. 1 Salamat Ali was deposing before the Court, he died on 17.7.85. Then the plaintiffs filed an application for substitution showing one Shamim Ahmed as son of deceased defendant No. 1 and the said application for substitution was allowed by the Court on 5.11.85. Then this petitioner defendant No. 1 (a) filed an application praying for setting aside the order dated 5.11.85 on the ground that deceased defendant No.1 Syed Salamat Ali had no son named Shamim Ahmed. After considering that application on 22.2.86 the trial Court kept that application in record holding that the said application would be considered at the time of final hearing of the suit.

3. Challenging that order dated 22.2.86, the present petitioner, namely, defendant No. 1 (a) moved a Revisional application before the High Court Division being CR No. 332 of 1986 and obtained a Rule. Ultimately, after hearing the Rule, the same was made absolute and the impugned order dated 22.2.86 was set aside. This court directed the trial" Court to consider first and decide as to whether Shamim Ahmed could be substituted as heir of deceased defendant No. 1 Syed Salamat Ali and whether the suit abated and after deciding this matter of substitution the suit would proceed in accordance with law. So, it was before the trial Court to consider as to whether Shamim Ahmed was the son of Syed Salamat Ali and whether the suit abated as a whole. After hearing the parties and considering the materials on record the learned Subordinate Judge passed the impugned order on 21.9.89 holding that the plaintiffs failed to prove that Shamim Ahmed was the son of defendant No.1 Syed Salamat Ali. It was further held that as the plaintiffs failed to substitute the alleged heir of deceased Syed Salamat Ali according to their own admission, the suit abated against deceased defendant No. 1 Syed Salamat Ali. But in the impugned order it has been held that although the suit abated, it would proceed against defendant No.1 (a), that is, the present petitioner in accordance with law. Being aggrieved by this portion of the order, that is, the suit would proceed against added defendant No. 1(a), the defendant No. 1(a), the present petitioner, moved this Revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure arid obtained the present Rule.

4. It may be mentioned that the plaintiffs did not challenge the impugned order of abatement as passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. They also did not challenge the impugned order by which the earlier order of substitution of Shamim Ahmed dated 5.11.85 had been set aside. So, the plaintiffs are bound by that order of abatement of the suit. Only point before us is to consider as to whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, the suit for specific performance of contract could be proceeded with against defendant No. 1 (a), namely, the present petitioner.

5. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that this is a suit for specific performance of contract and the suit shall proceed against only the necessary parties. Since the defendant No. l (a) is not a necessary party, the suit cannot be proceeded with against him. Mr. Islam further submits that the suit abated as a whole in view of the fact that the heirs of original defendant No.1 Syed Salamat Ali could not be substituted. Since the suit abated as a whole, it cannot be proceeded against defendant No. 1 (a). He further submits that suit in the present nature cannot be proceeded with in view of the provisions of section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as no legal title of the suit property passed to the present petitioner, defendant No. l(a), inasmuch as no deed of transfer was registered by the defendant Syed Salamat Ali in favour of the present petitioner. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that the suit can be proceeded against the present defendant No. 1(a) petitioner in accordance with the provisions of section 202 of the Contract Act inasmuch as the defendant No. 1 (a) has got the subsisting interest in the property as per contract and the power of attorney executed in favour of the defendant No. 1 (a) by defendant No. 1 and the consideration also passed from defendant No. 1 (a) to defendant No. 1.

6. We have gone through the impugned order. It appears to us that the learned Subordinate Judge has taken much pain to consider each and every aspect of the case and after considering the material evidence on record, he came to a conclusion that the suit abated against defendant No. 1. This portion of the order is going unchallenged which means the plaintiffs accepted that position of abatement of suit. Mr. Mahmudul Islam submits that since the suit abated against the deceased defendant No. 1 and since he is a necessary party in the present suit such a suit cannot be proceeded with in view of the fact that the court is unable to pass a decree in the suit of the present nature against a dead person. Mr. Islam has referred to section 27(b) of the Specific Relief Act which runs as follows:

27. Except as otherwise provided by this Chapter, specific performance of a contract may be enforced against.

......................................................................................................................

(b) Any other person claiming under him by a title arising to the contract, except a transferee for value who has paid his money in good faith and without notice of the original contract

.......................................................................................................................

<u>7. Mr. Islam submits that, from the power of attorney itself it appears that there was a contract in between the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 1 (a) and in pursuance of that contract the power of attorney was executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of the defendant No. 1 (a) and the consideration was allegedly passed to the defendant No. 1. Mr. Islam frankly submits that such a transaction may give some equitable right to the defendant No. 1 (a) to sue against the defendant No. 1, but such transaction will not create any legal title in the suit land in favour of the defendant No.1 (a). He submits that if the legal title does not pass to the defendant No. 1 (a), specific performance of contract cannot be enforced against the defendant No. 1(a), inasmuch as by this power of attorney no legal title has passed to the defendant No. 1 (a). In support of this contention Mr. Islam has referred to the case of Loknatn Prosad Singh vs. Shah Wahib Hussain AIR 1930 (pat) 181. In that case it was held by their Lordships of a Division Bench of Patna High Court that interpreting section 27(b) title of the suit property is very much relevant and unless the title passes to the subsequent transferee a decree for specific performance of contract cannot be enforced against him. Section 27 (b) of the Specific Relief Act is very clear to the effect that a decree for specific performance of contract cannot be enforced against a subsequent transferee unless the title of the suit property passes to the subsequent transferee. In the instant case it appears that by the contract as well as by the power of attorney, though consideration allegedly passed to the defendant No. 1 (a), the transaction cannot be called a sale or transfer of title to the subsequent transferee-defendant No. 1 (a). So we find substance in the contentions of Mr. Mahmudul Islam.</u>

8. Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that since interest has been created in favour of the subsequent transferee the defendant No. 1 (a) in respect of the suit property by virtue of a contract and power of attorney, the present suit can be proceeded with against the subsequent transferee namely Defendant No. 1 (a). In support of his contention, he has referred to section 202 of the Contract Act which runs as follows:

" 202. Termination of agency, where agent has an interest in subject-matter. Where the agent has himself an interest in the property which forms the subject-matter of the agency, the agency cannot, in the absence of an express contract, be terminated to the prejudice of such interest"

Relying on the provisions of section 202 of the Contract Act Mr. Fazlul Karim submits that since interest was created in favour of the subsequent transferee-defendant No. l (a) by virtue of the agreement as well as by the power of attorney, the suit can proceed against him. Mr. Mahmudul Islam frankly submits that the alleged contract and the power of attorney may create some equitable interest in favour of the defendant No. 1 (a), but that will not amount to passing of title to the subsequent transferee as contemplated under section 27 (b) of the Specific Relief Act. We find substance in the contentions of Mr. Islam. The point raised in the instant case should be considered in the light of the provisions of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as it is a suit for specific performance of contract and section 27 of the Specific Relief Act has clearly provided provisions for enforcement of a decree in a suit for specific performance of contract, So, the section 282 of the Contract Act is not of any assistance to Mr. Fazlul Karim.

9. Falzul Karim further submits that in the present suit if a decree is passed, the court will direct the defendant No. 1 (a) to execute and register the deed of sale in favour of the plaintiffs and if the defendant No. 1 (a) fails, the Court will execute and register the sale deed. Mr. Islam submits that in this case how this defendant No. 1 (a) will execute and register a sale deed in favour of the plaintiffs in respect of the suit property inasmuch as in the suit property the defendant No. 1 (a) has not acquired any title till now. A deed of sale can be executed and registered only by a person who has got legal title in the property. Since the defendant No. 1 (a), namely, the present petitioner has not acquired any legal title over the suit property, he is not in a position to execute and register a sale deed. So, Mr. Islam submits that a decree cannot be passed against the present petitioner defendant No. 1 (a) in the facts and circumstances of the case. We find substance in the above contention of Mr. Islam. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the provisions of law as discussed above, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order so far it relates to the finding that the suit will proceed against the defendant No. 1 (a). So, we hold that the present suit is not maintainable against defendant No. 1 (a), namely, the present petitioner.

In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the impugned order, so far it relates only to the portion that the present suit will continue against defendant No. 1 (a), is set aside. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment: Md. Ismailuddin Sarker J.: This appeal by leave by defendant No. 36 appellant raises a question of law as to whether the High Court Division was justified in interfering in revision with a finding of fact made by the trial Court in a proceeding under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as to non-service of summons upon the appellant. 2. Respondent No. 1 filed Title Suit No. 51 of 1970 in the Court of Subordinate Judge at Khulna for declaration of his title to the suit land measuring 11.64 acres. The suit was later on transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Satkhira and renumbered as Title Suit No. 514 of 1981. Amongst other defendants defendant No. 15 filed a written statement stating, inter alia. that he has sold some of the suit land to the appellant and others whereupon respondent No. 1 impleaded those purchasers as defendant Nos. 30-36. The suit was ultimately decreed ex parte on 28-1-1985. 3. Thereafter the appellant preferred Miscellaneous Case No. 79 of 1986 under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the ex parte decree on the grounds, inter alia, that no summons of the suit was served upon him which was fraudulently suppressed in collusion will the process server and he came to know about the ex parte decree on 27-7-1968 from one Binoy Krishna Bachar. He then went to the Court on 29.7.1986 and came to learn about the ex parte decree and thereafter filed the Miscellaneous Case. 4. Respondent No. 1 contested the miscellaneous case by filing a written objection denying the allegations of the petitioner and contending, inter alia, that the summons was duly served upon the appellant and that there was no suppression of the summons and the suit was decreed in due course. 5. The appellant examined three PWs. including himself and the respondent No. 1 examined two DWs. including himself. In view of Order No.89 dated 25-3-1976 passed by the Subordinate Judge; Khulna in the suit stating that defendant Nos. 30-36 appeared by separate vokalatnamas and filed separate petitions praying for adopting the written statement filed by defendant No. 15 which was allowed, the learned Subordinate Judge, Satkhira directed the Bench Assistant to file a report. The Bench Assistant filed his report on 29-8-1988 stating, inter alia, that although the summons which were served upon the defendants were mentioned in the firisti there was no mention of the summons upon the appellant in the firisti. The learned Subordinate Judge noticed that though it was recorded in Order No.89 dated 25-3-1976 by the Subordinate Judge, Khulna that the appellant appeared in the suit by filing vokalatnama no vokalatnama was found with the record nor there was any mention of the summons in the name of the appellant in the firisti. The learned Subordinate Judge also compared the admitted signatures of the appellant with his alleged signature in the petition for adopting the written statement of defendant No.I5 by him Considering the evidence on record and the record of the case, the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 30-11-1988 allowed the miscellaneous case and set aside the ex parte decree on condition of payment of Taka 300.00 as costs by the appellant on the finding that no summons was served upon the appellant and that he came to learn about the ex parte decree for the rust time on the date as alleged by him. 6. Against the aforesaid order of the Subordinate Judge setting aside the ex parte decree respondent No. 1 moved the High Court Division in revision and obtained a Rule in Civil Revision No. 166 of 1989 (Jessore), renumbered as Civil Revision No. 3778 of 1991 (Dhaka). 7. A learned Single Judge of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order dated 3-7-1994 made the Rule absolute and setting aside the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the ex parte decree. 8. Mr. SS Halder, learned Counsel appeared on behalf of the appellant and submitted that the learned Judge of the High Court Division had committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice in reversing the finding of fact arrived at by the trial Court in revision without considering that the trial Court came to the finding after thorough enquiry into the matter and the evidence on record, in particular, the report submitted by the Bench Assistant. There is substance in the contention of the learned Counsel for the appellant. 9. Mr. A M Rahim, learned Advocate- on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1, could not furnish any satisfactory explanation as to non-mentioning of the summons upon the appellant in the firisti filed in the suit. (as per report of the Bench Assistant). 10. In an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the ex parte decree the whole onus is upon the plaintiff to prove that summons was duly served upon the defendant. Respondent No.1 failed to prove by adducing cogent evidence that summons was duly served upon the appellant, Although the learned Judge of the High Court Division noticed that the return of the summons alleged to have been served upon the appellant and the vokalatnama alleged to have been filed by the appellant were missing from the record gave much stress to the order dated 25-3-1976 and without considering the report submitted by the Bench Assistant erroneously found that the trial Court was wrong in holding that summons was not served upon the appellant. The learned Judge of the High Court Division also erred in law in holding that the trial Court was wrong-in comparing the signature of the appellant appearing in the alleged application dated 25-3-1976 with his admitted signatures. Rather, the learned Judge of the High Court Division exceeded his jurisdiction in revision in entering into a question of fact and in comparing the signatures himself to arrive at a contrary finding of fact. The finding of fact as to non-service of summons made by the trial Court was not perverse, nor was it such as could legitimately justify an interference by the revisional Court on accepted principles. For the reasons stated above the judgment and order of the learned Judge of the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. In the result, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs. End.

vs. 
Chairman, Board of Directors, Agrani Bank, Head Office, Dhaka & others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated 31-7-94 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 59 of 1993).
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal J: This appeal by leave by the petitioner-appellant is from the Judgment and order dated 31-7-94 passed by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 59 of 1993 dismissing the appellant's appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 15-5-93 passed by the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka in Administrative Tribunal Case No. 27 of 1989, dismissing the appellant's application under section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981, henceforth the said Act.

2. The appellant, a Manager in the Audit Division of the Head Office, Agrani Bank, respondent No. 2 was departmentally proceeded against by a charge-sheet dated 8-11-77 following which he was dismissed from service on 16-2-79, an appeal from which order was also rejected by the Chairman. Board of Directors of the said Bank on 21-12-81. He filed Title Suit No. 109 of 1982 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka which on transfer to the court of Subordinate Judge and Commercial Court, Dhaka was renumbered as Title Suit No. 72 of 1984. By a judgment and decree dated 28-3-85 the appellant's suit was decreed and the impugned orders dated 16-2-79 and 11-12-81 were declared to be void, illegal and without jurisdiction and the plaintiff was declared to be still in service in the eye of law with loss of 3 years seniority in service. The respondent bank preferred Title Appeal No. 94 of 1985 and the appellant also filed a cross appeal. The respondent's appeal was dismissed and the appellant's cross-appeal was allowed by judgment and decree dated 28-4-86 passed by the 3rd Court of Additional District Judge, Dhaka. The trial Court's decree was modified thereby. The decree of loss of 3 years seniority in service was deleted. The appellant joined his services on 28-4-86 and he submitted an application on 20-12-86 to the Chairman, Board of Directors of the Bank, respondent No.1 for arrear pay and other financial benefits where after he was informed on 7-9-89 that his prayer had been rejected by the Board. The appellant then filed case No. 27 of 1989 on 29-1-89 before the Administrative Tribunal. Dhaka, claiming as many as nine reliefs mainly concerning his arrear pay, etc. from 16-2-79 to 13-8-86, scale of pay, promotion and other benefits. The Administrative Tribunal dismissed the appellant's case solely on the ground that the reliefs claimed for emanate from the Civil Court's decree and are in the nature of ancillary and consequential reliefs arising out of the Civil Court's decree. The appellant by putting the decree into execution in the Civil Court under the saving clause provided in section 13 of the Administrative Tribunals Act 1980 can ask for execution of the decree from the same Court which passed the decree. The petition was held to be not maintainable before the Tribunal. The merit of the appellant's case was not gone into.

3. On appeal the Appellant Tribunal concurred with the opinion of the Administrative Tribunal and, as already noticed, dismissed the appeal.

<u>4. Leave was granted on the submissions that the Tribunals below erred in not considering that the cause of action of the appellant before the Tribunal arose not because the appellant was praying for some ancillary or consequential reliefs following the decree of the Civil Court, but because the Board of Directors of the respondent bank illegally refused his prayer for arrear salary and other reliefs in violation of the decisions laid down in the cases of Government of Bangladesh vs. Md. Mustafa and others 35 DLR 404, Saleh Ahmed Joarder vs. People's Republic of Bangladesh, 36 DLR (AD) 26 and Executive Engineer, Public Health, Barisal Division vs. Mohammad Ali, 41 DLR (AD) 64 and thus erred in law in not holding that the appellant's application before the Tribunal is founded upon a new cause of action, hence maintainable.</u>

5. Mr. Shafique Ahmed, learned Counsel for the appellant, placed before us the plaint and judgment of Title Suit No. 72 of 1984. In the plaint the appellant prayed for a declaration that the orders dated 16-2-79 and 21-12-81 are void, illegal, without jurisdiction, malafide, inoperative and without lawful authority and that the plaintiff (appellant) is still in service in the eye of law. In the judgment of the trial Court in Title Suit No. 72 of 1984 it was ordered as follows:

"That the suit be decreed on contest against the defendant without any order dated 16-2-79 passed by the defendant No. 1 dismissing the plaintiff from service and the order dated 11-12-81 passed by the defendants 2 and 3 are void, illegal, without jurisdiction and the plaintiff is still in service in the eye of law but the plaintiff will lose 3 years' seniority in service."

6. In Title Appeal No. 94 of 1985 passed by the 3rd Court of Additional District Judge Dhaka the final order is as follows:

“অতএব আদেশ হই যে, অত্র আপীল মামলা দোতরফা সূত্রে ময় খরচে ডিসমিস হইল। উক্ত মর্মে নিম্ন আদালতের রায় বহাল রহিল তবে উপরোক্ত আলোচনার মর্মানুসারে নিম্ন আদালত কর্তৃক জনাব নজীবের ৩ বৎসরের সিনিউরিটি বিনিষ্ট করা সংক্রান্ত আদেশ বাতিল করা গেল।”

7. Mr. Shafique Ahmed submits that in pursuance of the Appellate Court's decree the appellant joined his services on 28-4-86. As such, the appellate decree was fully executed and there remained nothing for the trial Court to execute anything further in pursuance of the decree obtained by the appellant. What the appellant submitted to the Chairman, Board of Directors of the respondent Bank by his representation dated 20-12-86 were neither ancillary nor consequential reliefs granted or to be granted in pursuance of the decree obtained by the appellant. Mr. Shafique Ahmed then placed before us the appellant's representation dated 20-12-86. He claimed absorption in the new National Pay Scale of Taka 1400.00-2225.00. He also claimed promotion as a matter of right in respect of officers of category and was aggrieved by his placement as Grade-V Senior Officer carrying the new scale of pay of Taka 425-1275.00 instead of his proper scale of pay of Taka 1400-2225.00 He claimed that he sustained a loss of Taka 3.67.039.00 due to his illegal dismissal from 16-2-79 to 13-8-86 which he also claimed to be paid as his salary and allowances. All these grievances relate to service benefits, namely, promotion, fixation of correct scale of pay, status, position and seniority in service. These reliefs were neither claimed in the plaint nor decreed. As such, he submits, both the Tribunals below committed an illegality in holding that the representation as aforesaid was made for allowing the appellant's service benefits as per judgment and decree of the Civil Court and that the Tribunal case was instituted for enforcement of those rights and consequential benefits arising out of the judgment and decree of the Civil Court. Mr, Shafique Ahmed further submits that both the Tribunals erred in law in holding that in the facts of the present case the Tribunals have no authority to execute a decree of a Civil Court and that the application in the form instituted is not maintainable. The Tribunals below have also misinterpreted section 13 of the said Act.

8. Mr. Syed Abdur Rahim, learned Counsel for the respondent-Bank, in re-reading the appellant's representation dated 20-12-86 points out that the appellant himself stated variously at various places in the said representation that the claims that he was putting forward were in terms of the judgment and decree of the Civil Court. That appears to be correct, but the refusal of the respondent-Bank contained in its letter dated 7-1-89 was specifically on the ground inter alia, that in the judgment of the Civil Court there was no direction to the respondent-Bank to confer on the appellant's promotion and other service benefits now being asked for by the appellant after his re-instatement.

9. This is the root cause of refusal of the appellant's representation and therefore the moot point is, whether the appellant will go to the Civil Court for execution of the decree or will file an application to the Administrative Tribunal for redress of his grievances.

10. Mr. Syed Abdur Rahim, upon hearing the learned Counsel for the appellant, now finds it difficult to support the views of the two Tribunals that the appellant's remedy lies in executing the decree of the Civil Court because, as Mr. Shafique Ahmed rightly submitted, after the appellant was re-instated in service, there remained nothing by way of execution of the Civil Court's decree which was merely declaratory in nature.

11. Both the Tribunals below have relied upon section 13 of the said Act which is as follows:

13. "Savings-All suits, cases, applications and appeals relating to any matter in respect of which a Tribunal has jurisdiction pending, immediately before the commencement of this Act, before any court shall be tried, heard and disposed of by such Court, as if this Act had not come into force."

<u>12. It is obvious that section 13 of the said Act has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the present case. The decree of the Civil Courts having already been executed after the appellant was re-instated in service, his subsequent prayer for promotion, status, scale of pay, arrear pay and other benefits do not fall in the category of any pending suit, case, application and appeal pending immediately before the commencement of the said Act This is a new cause of action arising after the commencement of the said Act and the appellant has correctly invoked the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal for obtaining relief in the matter prayed for. The two Tribunals apparently took a wrong view that these relief are ancillary and consequential reliefs emanating from the decree of the Civil Court and have wrongly refrained from exercising their jurisdiction in the matter.</u>

The appeal is allowed with costs and remanded to the Administrative Tribunal for hearing the case in accordance with law.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.209 of 1997.
lawyer:
Md Fazlul Karim, Senior Advocate, instructed by Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ---- For the Petitioner. 
Not represented ---- Respondents.
parties:
Abdul Kaiyum (Md) ----- Plaintiff-Petitioner
vs. 
Krishnadhan Banik being dead, his heirs Bijan kumar Banik and others ----- Respondents
case_source: (From the judgment and order dated November 27 1996 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Civil Revision No.1408 of 1995).
full_judgment:
ATM Afzal CJ: The plaintiff-petitioner's prayer for temporary injunction was rejected concurrently by the Courts below and the High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order dated 27 November, 1996 passed in Civil Revision No.1408 of 1995, refused to interfere with the said decision. Now this petition for leave to appeal from the same.

2. Facts of the case, briefly, are that the petitioner filed Title Suit No.17 of 1991 in the Fourth Court of Assistant Judge, Narayanganj against respondent Nos.2-5 for specific performance of contract. The suit was decreed on compromise on 12-11-91 and in execution of the said decree, Title Execution Case No.2 of 1991, the petitioner got possession of the disputed property on 18-2-94. On 1-3-94 the predecessor of respondent Nos.1(a)-1(f), Krishnadhan Banik, who was not a party to Title Suit No.17 of 1991, filed an application under rule 100 of Order XXI of the Code of Civil Procedure, Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 1994, complaining that he had been illegally dispossessed from the property in execution of the decree passed in Title Suit No.17 of 1991. The said Misc. case having been allowed by judgment and order dated 14-7-1994, the petitioner instituted Title Suit No.83 of 1994 under rule 103 of Order XXI CPC which is now pending. The petitioner prayed for an order of temporary injunction restraining defendant, Krishnadhan Banik, from taking delivery of possession of the property in execution of the judgment and order passed in Miscellaneous Case No.6 of 1994. As already noticed, the prayer was rejected both by the trial Court and the appellate Court.

3. The High Court Division upon noticing the provisions of rules 101 and 103 of Order XXI CPC interpreted the said rules holding:

"We find that the word "shall" used in rule 101 indicate that the successful applicant must be put into possession and words "present possession" in rule 103 mean that the plaintiff in a suit filed thereunder shall have to establish his claim to get the present possession and do not mean that he shall have to establish his claim to retain his present possession, that is to say, the decree-holder has to file the suit under rule 102 for possession for deciding the question of title because in a case under rule 101 the executing court can deal only with bonafide possession of a third party dispossessed in execution of a decree and the third party, if successful, must be put into possession."

4. In such view of the matter, the Rule was discharged, that is to say, the rejection of the payer for temporary injunction was affirmed.

<u>5. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for the petitioner, has submitted that the High Court Division put a wrong interpretation on rule 103 suggesting that a suit under this rule is maintainable only when possession of the immoveable property is delivered to the third party as per the order passed under rule 101. We find nothing of the kind putting bar on a suit under rule 103 in the impugned order as argued by Mr. Karim. We agree with the view taken by the High Court Division that the applicant has to be put back into possession of the disputed property as mandated by rule 101 notwithstanding the suit filed under rule 103 to establish the right of the plaintiff to the present possession of the property. In other words, the direction under rule 101 cannot be held back on the ground of institution of a suit under rule 103.</u>

<u>6. Mr. Karim has then argued that in view of the fact that Krishnadhan Banik filed application under rule 100 the learned Judges ought to have held that the order passed under rule 101 was illegal inasmuch as relief was granted to respondent in respect of moveable property. We are not prepared for a surprise argument like this because it does not find place either in the impugned judgment or in the revision petition before the High Court Division.</u>

The petition is dismissed.

End.

Rahima Khatun ------ Petitioner

Md Nurul Hoque & others ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 12-2-96 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Laksam Thana Assistant Judge's Court at Comilla in Miscellaneous Case No.35 of 1995, setting aside the ex parte preliminary decree dated 24-4-95 passed in Partition Suit No.12 of 1992.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff instituted Partition Suit No. 128 of 1984 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge Comilla, for partition of the suit properties and to allot her a saham for her legal share inherited by her from her mother Rabiya Khatun.

3. The defendant Nos. 12-18 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement. The suit was thereafter transferred to the court of Assistant Judge, Laksam for hearing and disposal and it was re-numbered as Partition Suit No. 12 of 1994. The defendant No.18 Osman Gani who was one of the contesting defendants died in 1994 and his heirs opposite party Nos. 1-9 were not substituted by the plaintiffs. Thereafter the suit was decreed ex patre in the preliminary form on 24-4-95. Then plaintiff made a prayer for appointment of a commissioner to effect partition and the commissioner after visiting the suit properties prepared a map, Chitta, Saham book and submitted the same before the trial Court. Thereafter, the opposite party Nos. 1-9, the heirs of deceased defendant No. 18, filed Miscellaneous Case No. 35 of 1995 under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree on the ground that their predecessor-in-interest Osman Gani died long ago and they were not made party and no notice was served upon them. They came to know about the ex parte decree only on 26-6-95.

4. The plaintiff opposite party No. 1 contested the aforesaid miscellaneous case contending, inter alia, that the aforesaid miscellaneous case is misconceived and not maintainable under the provisions of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as they were not the defendants in the suit and ex parte decree has not been passed either against their father or themselves. It was further contended that the aforesaid miscellaneous case is hopelessly barred by limitation.

5. The petitioner as well as the opposite party Nos. 1-9 examined one witness from each side in support of their respective cases and the learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment and order dated 12-2-96 allowed the miscellaneous case and being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order the plaintiff petitioner obtained the instant Rule.

6. Mr Abdul Kuddus Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner, submits that the trial Court committed a patent illegality in entertaining the miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure inasmuch as the aforesaid application does not come within the ambit of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure inasmuch as Order 9 rule 13 of the Code contemplates that only a defendant against whom an ex parte decree is passed can file an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree and in that view of the matter the trial Court taking an erroneous view of law illegally entertained the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and subsequently allowed the same. The second plank of attack made by Mr Abdul Kuddus Miah is that the decree passed against a dead person is a nullity and had no existence in the eye of law and in the instant case admittedly the ex parte preliminary decree was passed against defendant No. 18 when he was no more alive and, as such, the decree so far it relates to the defendant No. 18 is a nullity in the eye of law and Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure entitles a defendant to file an application to set aside an ex parte decree which has rightly been passed by the trial Court and in the instant case since admittedly the defendant No. 18 the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite party Nos. 1-9, was not alive, the preliminary decree in question is a nullity and in that view of the matter the instant application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure filed by the opposite party Nos. 1-9 before the Court is absolutely misconceived and not tenable in law. In support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1923 (All) 30.

7. Mr M Enayetur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1-9, on the other hand, submits that their father figured as defendant No. 18 in the partition suit and he along with other defendants namely, defendant Nos. 12-17 jointly filed a written statement in order to contest the suit but during the pendency of the suit he died in 1984 and his heirs were not brought on record by the plaintiff petitioner at any point of time and subsequently the preliminary decree was passed on 24-4-95 and the opposite party Nos. 1-9 came to know about the ex parte decree on 25-6-95 and filed the miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code for setting aside the ex parte decree which has been passed against their dead father. The learned Advocate further submits that as heirs of defendant No. 18 they are affected by the ex parte preliminary decree and, as such, they are entitled to invoke the provisions of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code.

8. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the contention raised by the plaintiff petitioner before this court were also agitated before the trial Court and the trial Court repelled their contentions holding that the opposite party Nos. 1-9 as legal representatives of deceased defendant No.18 are very much entitled to invoke the jurisdiction of the court through an application filed under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code.

9. In the course of his argument Mr Abdul Kuddus Miah has submitted that since the preliminary decree in question is a nullity so far it relates to the defendant No. 18, the, opposite party Nos. 1-9 have their remedy and they can get the relief by instituting an independent suit for declaration that the decree in question passed by the trial Court is a nullity in the eye of law and since they were not defendants in the suit they have no locaus standi to file the Miscellaneous Case. I have perused the decision referred to and relied on by Mr Miah reported in AIR 1923 (All) 30. In that case the decree was passed ex parte against one Shafatullah who applied for the setting aside of such decree. He died and his legal representatives were brought on the record. The application was dismissed by the trial Court and on appeal the learned District Judge dismissed the appeal on the ground that the right to set aside a decree passed ex parte is given to a defendant against whom a decree is passed and his legal representatives have no right to set it aside. Against that order a revision was preferred before the Allahabad High Court and a Division Bench of that Court allowed the revision and observed that, "It would be a monstrous state of things if it were the law that the heirs, or legal personal representatives, could not as of right pursue any claim which a deceased man had, which death had prevented him from pursuing" and their Lordships further observed that the decision reported in (1899) 21 All 274 is no more good law in view of the provisions of section 146 which was clearly enacted to cover a case like this.

10. Mr Miah relied on this case and distinguished the present case on the ground that in that case the defendant was alive when the decree was passed and in the instant case the defendant was dead when the preliminary decree in question was passed. It is admitted by both the sides that the defendant No.18 was dead on 24-4-95 when the preliminary decree was passed and in that view of the matter it is also admitted that the decree so far relates to the defendant No. 18 is a nullity. Now the main question that calls for determination in this case is as to whether the heirs of defendant No. 18 can invoke the provisions of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code or they must resort to other remedies that are available to them in view of the facts and circumstances of the case.

<u>11. It is now well settled that against an ex parte decree a surviving defendant has two remedies he can file an application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code for setting aside the ex parte decree or if he so chooses can follow both the remedies simultaneously and the settled position of law is that if the appeal is heard earlier then the miscellaneous case will become infructuous and if the miscellaneous case is heard rust then the appeal will become infructuous but there is no legal barrier imposed by law on a defendant in pursuing the said remedies simultaneously. It entirely depends on the choice of the defendant In that view of the matter in the instant case also had the defendant No.18 been alive on the date of passing the ex parte decree he could either file an application under Order 9 rule 13 or could file an appeal against the ex parte decree or could pursue both the remedies simultaneously. If that be so why the heirs who have stepped into the shoes of the defendant No.18 after his death shall be deprived of these legal remedies and I again quote the expression used by their Lordships of the Allahabad High Court in the decision reported in AIR 1923 (All) 30 that "it would be a monstrous state of things if it were the law that the heirs, or legal personal representatives, could not as of right pursue any claim which a deceased man had, which death had prevented him from pursuing." Besides, section 146, CPC is as follows:</u>

<u>"Save as otherwise provided by this Code or by any law for the time being in force, where any proceeding may be taken or application made by or against any person, then the proceeding may be taken or the application may be made by or against any person claiming under him."</u>

<u>It is thus clear that, as stated in the section, it is a case where an application could have been made by the deceased father of the opposite party Nos. 1-9 and, as such, the section authorises the opposite party Nos. 1-9 who are claiming under defendant No.18 to make the application which could have been filed by their deceased father. Here it may further be mentioned that an application under Order 9 rule 13 is not exempted from the general provision relating to procedure contained in section 146. A legal representative can therefore file an application to set aside an ex parte decree before he is actually brought on the record. That being the legal position, a legal representative of a deceased defendant is entitled to file an application under Order 9, rule 13 to set aside an ex parte decree irrespective of the fact as to whether the deceased defendant had died before or after the ex parte decree is passed.</u>

12. In the instant case it is admitted that defendant No. 18 died in 1984 and the heirs were not brought on record by substitution and the preliminary decree was passed long after his death. The preliminary decree was obtained by suppressing that fact. The heirs of defendant No. 18 could have taken appropriate steps in the suit before passing of the preliminary decree had they been brought on record in time and if they are not allowed now to file an application under Order 9, rule 13 the plaintiff will be allowed to take advantage of his own fraud and law cannot allow that. Thus, I do not find any substance in this revisional application.

13. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

14. The order of stay earlier granted by this court is hereby vacated.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 2.8.93 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal Nos.181 of 1990 and 30 of 1992).
full_judgment: Mustafa Kamal J: These two appeals by leave have been preferred by Bangladesh from the common judgment and decree of the High Court Division dated 2.8.93 in First Appeal Nos. 181 of 1990 and 30 of 1992 dismissing both. 2 . Admittedly, the suit property, to wit, a two-storied building with other tin shed and structures being House No. 145A. Road No.2 Dhanmondi Residential Area, Police Station—Lalbagh, District—Dhaka standing on 1 bigha of land or there-about, originally belonged to one Dr. S M Shamim, who took a loan from Rupali Bank (the then Muslim Commercial Bank) on 26.6.70 and on his failure to repay the loan Rupali Bank obtained an ex parte decree on 26.7.72 against Dr. Shamim in Money Suit No. 32 of 1972 from the 3rd Court of Munsif Dhaka for realisation of the loan amount. Rupali Bank started Money Execution Case No. 32 of 1972 against the judgment-debtor and the suit property was attached on 21.12.72 and was advertised for sale in auction in the 'Dainik Bangla'. The appellant, Bangladesh, preferred Miscellaneous Case No.174 of 1974in the Execution Case, under Order XXI rule 58 CPC praying of release for the suit property from attachment on the ground that it was an abandoned property. Rupali Bank filed a written objection, but the appellant's Miscellaneous Case No.174 was dismissed on 25.2.77. A fresh sale proclamation was published in the 'Daily 'adage on 5.2.78 and the suit property was sold in auction on 7.3.78. Respondent No.1 Md. Suruzzamal was the highest bidder at Taka 1,21,500.00 which was deposited by him in Court by two treasury chalans dated 9.9.78 and 20.3.78. The sale was confirmed on 17.4.78 and the Court issued sale certificate to the auction-purchaser under Order XXI rule 94 CPC, on 17.3.79. The auction purchaser also got symbolical possession of the suit property on 4.6.79 through Court by beat of drums in presence of witnesses. 3. The auction purchaser admittedly found appellant-Bangladesh and Director-General. Radio Bangladesh to be in possession of the suit property and he filed an application to the Minister of Public Works and urban Development in 20.6.79 for releasing the suit property in his favour being a lawful auction-purchaser thereof. 4. Instead of granting any relief to the auction-purchaser Bangladesh as plaintiff instituted in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge. Dhaka Title Suit No.69 of 1981 on 18.2.81 against the auction-purchaser for declaration of title to the suit property on the allegations inter alia that Dr. S M Shamim was a non-local. He left Bangladesh during the war of liberation and his whereabouts were not known after liberation. The suit property thus became an abandoned property within the meaning of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 gad it vested in the Government on and from 28.2.7/2. M an abandoned property the suit property was allotted to the Director-General, Radio Bangladesh for office accommodation in July, 1972 from which date the suit property is in possession or the said Director-General, Radio Bangladesh as an allottee under the Government. In June, 1979 respondent No.1 filed an application to the Minister of Public Works and urban Development asserting that the suit property is not an abandoned property and it has not vested in the Government and narrating how he auction purchased the suit property and obtained symbolical possession. The plaintiff contended that the suit property was exempt from any legal process including attachment or sale by any Court and there-fore the attachment and sale was illegal and without lawful authority. The plaintiff was not a party either to Money suit No. 32 of 1972 or to the Execution Case and the right, title and interest of Bangladesh has not passed to the auction purchaser. As the alleged auction purchase has cast a cloud on the plaintiff's title to the suit property, so the suit. 5. Before filing a written statement in the aforesaid title suit No. 69 of 1981, the auction-purchaser filed title suit No.339 of 1981 on 11.7.81 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge. Dhaka narrating substantially what has been stated above and claiming further that the suit property was never declared as an abandoned property and never vested in Bangladesh. Both Bangladesh and Director-General, Radio Bangladesh are in unauthorised occupation of the suit property without any right, title and interest. It was asserted that Dr. Shamim was a Bangladeshi National and he had his permanent residence in the city of Dhaka and he was living at Dhaka althrough out. In his suit the auction-purchaser made Bangladesh, Director-General of Radio Bangladesh and Rupali Bank as defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 3 respectively and prayed for a declaration of his 16 annas right, title and interest in the suit.property and also for a decree to remove defendant Nos. 1 and 2 their officers, agents, assigns and servants from the suit property and to deliver khas possession thereof to him. 6. On 25.7.81 the auction-purchaser filed a written statement in Title suit No. 69 of 1981 denying the plaintiff's case and asserting substantially the same statements which he had made in the plaint of Title Suit No. 339 of 1981. 7 . On 23.7.84 Bangladesh and Director-General, Radio Bangladesh as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed a joint written statement in Title Suit No.339 of 1981, stating substantially the same which the plaintiff stated in the plaint of Title Suit No.69 of 1981. 8. The two suits were analogously heard by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, Bangladesh as plaintiff examined one witness, but produced no documents and the auction-purchaser examined 4 witnesses and produced some documents in support of his auction purchase. By a common judgment and decree dated 31.8.88 the learned Sub-ordinate Judge decreed Title Suit No. 339 of 1981 filed by the auction-purchaser and dismissed Title Suit No.69 of 1981 filed by Bangladesh. 9. Bangladesh thereafter preferred FA No. 181 of 1990 and FA No. 30 of 1992 against the judgment and decree in Title Suit No.339 of 1981 and Title Suit No.69 of 1981 respectively before the High Court Division. 10. As already noticed, the High Court Division by the impugned judgment dismissed both the appeals. 11. Leave was granted to consider the submission of the appellant that the trial Court and the High Court Division fell into an error in not considering the facts, circumstances and evidence in the case properly, keeping in view the definition of "abandoned property" as in President's Order No. 16 of 1972, which resulted in an erroneous decision causing a miscarriage of justice. Further contention on which leave has been granted is that there is clear evidence that the original owner of the suit property was not present and managing the same on the promulgation of President's Order No. 16 of 1972, that the original owner having not raised any claim in respect of the suit property at any stage and that the suit property having been admittedly in the possession of Radio Bangladesh since July, 1972 as an allottee from the Government as an abandoned property, there is no escape from the conclusion that the suit property is an abandoned property which was exempt from all legal process and as such the respondent acquired no title on the basis of auction sale. Leave was also granted to consider whether the High Court Division rightly relied on some decisions of this Division and the High Court Division and whether it failed to rely on some more appropriate decisions of this Division. 12. At the time of granting leave Mr. TH Khan, entering Caveat for the auction-purchaser orally objected to CA No. 15 of 1994 as time-barred and prayed for keeping the question of limitation open at the hearing of the appeal, which was allowed. 13. Mr. AW Bhuiyan, learned Additional Attorney-General appearing for the appellant submits that Rupali Bank filed Money Suit No.32 of 1972 against Dr. Shamim on 3.5.72 in the 3rd Court of Munsif at Dhaka. The suit property was shown to be the address of Dr. Shamim for service of summons in the suit in the suit. He did not enter appearance. The plaint of the said suit reveals that Dr. Shamim took a loan of Taka 10,000.00 from Rupali Bank on 26.6.70. He repaid nearly all the outstanding dues except Taka 3,098.00 for realisation of which the Bank filed the suit. There is absolutely no explanation as to why he did not appear in the suit if he was present in Bangladesh and residing in the suit property. Also there is no explanation why he did not resist the sale of a two storied building on one bigha of land for a paltry outstanding due of Taka 3,098.00 if he was present at Dhaka althroughout. It is asserted by all the witnesses examined by the auction-purchaser that Dr. Shamim was a well known physician and the witnesses knew him because he treated them, but none of them stated that they found Dr. Shamim occupying, managing and supervising the suit property since liberation. On the contrary, he submits, PW 1 Haji Andur Rouf and PW 4 Abdul Mannan Chowdhury, examined by the auction-purchaser, admitted in cross-examination that the suit property is in possession of Radio Bangladesh as an office since liberation of Bangladesh. Deposing in 1988 all the witnesses of the auction-purchaser asserted that Dr. Shamim was a Bangalee and PW 1, PW 3 (the auction-purchaser himself) and PW 2 Md. Sekandar Ali Miah asserted in one voice that Dr. Shamim was present in Bangladesh even in 1988. Both the trial Court and the High Court Division uncritically accepted this evidence, without taking into consideration the fact that a Bangladeshi national living in the City of Dhaka althroughout and finding his own valuable residential property to be sold out in auction for a sum of Taka 1,21,500.00 without any objection or resistance from him is not a common course of human conduct. The suit property is admittedly in possession of Radio Bangladesh since July, 1972. Dr. Shamim, if ever he was present in Bangladesh, could have moved the proper authorities under President's Order No.16 of 1972 for relesase of his property. But he is totally out of scene since 1972 upto the present date. Even though the auction-purchaser claimed that he saw Dr. Shamim at Dhaka he did not examine Dr. Shamim. The sole witness examined by the appellant in Title Suit No.69 of 1981, PW 1 Md. Syed Kamal Ali clearly asserted in his examination-in-chief that Dr. Shamim is a non-Bangalee, that he was absent from 28.2.72, that the house was declared as an abandoned property and that the Director-General of Radio Bangladesh is in possession of the suit property. The learned Additional Attorney-General submits that without adverting to these circumstances, evidence and facts of the case both the trial Court and the High Court Division harped on the theme that the suit property was not an abandoned property because no list is forthcoming to show that it was enlisted as an abandoned property. He submits that the enlistment of a property in the list of abandoned properties is not the criterion for determining whether a property is abandoned or not. He refers to the definition of 'abandoned property' in Article 2(1) of President's Order No.16 of 1972 and submits that if the owner is not present in Bangladesh or if his whereabouts are not known or if he has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property then the property becomes ipso facto an abandoned property whether it is enlisted in a list compiled by the relevant Ministry or not. In the present case, he submits, there is only some oral evidence that Dr. Shamim was present in Bangladesh, rendered totally useless by the fact that at no stage he claimed restoration of his property and allowed a valuable property to be sold in auction for a paltry claim of Taka 3,098.00 There is also oral evidence that he was present in Bangladesh, but regard being had to the fact that he never showed up at any stage after 1972 this evidence is absolutely unworthy of consideration, he submits. He finally submits that there is absolutely no evidence, even by the witnesses of the auction-purchaser, that Dr. Shamim occupied, supervised or managed in person the suit property before or after President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force. On the contrary, the witnesses examined by the auction-purchaser openly acknowledged that Radio Bangladesh was in possession of the suit property since liberation. The learned Additional Attorney-General therefore submits that both the Courts below failed to examine the facts and circumstances of the case properly and employed an extra-legal yardstick, namely, enlistment of property, for determining whether the suit property was abandoned or not without keeping in view the definition of abandoned property in President's Order No. 16 of 1972. 14. Mr. TH 'Khan, learned Counsel for the auction-purchaser respondent No. 1 submits on the other hand that the two Courts below in a concurrent assessment of the evidence on record found as a fact that D. Shamim was present in Bangladesh. He is a Bangladeshi National and therefore the suit property cannot be treated as an abandoned property. The High Court Division has additionally found that the appellant failed to produce any document or paper in the trial Court to show that the property was declared or enlisted as an abandoned property. These two concurrent findings of fact, he submits should not be disturbed unless the treatment of evidence by the two Courts below is so pernicious and shocking to conscience that this Court is impelled to interfere. 15. Before the High Court Division the appellant filed the letter of allotment to Radio Bangladesh dated 11.7.72 with an application for admitting the same as an additional evidence. The High Court Division did not formally admit the same as an additional evidence nor did it dispose of that application by rejecting the application. On the other hand, the High Court Division took the letter of allotment into consideration, but held that this letter cannot be the foundation of treating the property as an abandoned property when no survey report or list of abandoned property or any paper was filed to show that there was determination that the property was an abandoned property. Mr. TH Khan submits that the High Court Division correctly treated the matter from the right perspective and the same is not liable to interference. 16. Having given our most anxious consideration to the submissions of both sides we cannot but hold that the two Courts below have sorely missed the yardstick with which to determine whether a property is an abandoned property or not. A property is an Abandoned Property if it falls within the definition of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. In this particular case the owner himself is not coming forward to assert that he was present in Bangladesh all along. In the case relied upon by the High Court Division namely, M/s Khan Brothers Ltd. vs Government of Bangladesh 27 DLR 423, an artificial person namely a private limited company itself challenged a Gazette Notification taking over the management of its properties and assets under Articles 4 and 5 of President's Order No.16 of 1972. In the other case relied upon by the High Court Division Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs. M/s Speedbird Navigation Co. 30 DLR (SC) 101, five Banladeshi partners of the firm representing 75% interest of the firm challenged the Notifications taking over their properties for management. In the last case felled upon by the High Court Division, Bangladesh vs Messrs ATJ Industries Ltd. 28 DLR (AD) 120, it is the share-holders who challenged the taking over of the management of the properties of a private limited company. In the present case the real owner being totally absent from the legal proceedings instituted against him since 1972 and having not made any representation to the Government for restoration of his property the onus on the Government to prove that the owner was not present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were not known or he has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, is a negative one, meaning thereby that the Government do not have to adduce positive evidence of those facts. A mere assertion will do in the facts and circumstances of the case which the appellant through PW 1 Md. Syed Kamal Ali has done. The auction-purchaser's witnesses, on the other hand, have only orally asserted that Dr. Shamim was a Bangalee, that he was present in Bangladesh althroughout and that he was present in Bangladesh even in 1988. No certificate has been produced to show that he was a Bangladeshi National. No evidence has been given that Dr. Shamim was in possession of the suit property on or before 28.2.72. No address of Dr. Shamim has been given to prove that his whereabouts were known. There is no assertion by any of these witnesses that Dr. Shamim occupied, supervised or managed in person his property. On the contrary, it is these witnesses themselves who admitted that Radio Bangladesh was in possession of the suit property since the liberation of Bangladesh. The High Court Division unnecessarily shifted the onus on the appellant to prove that it enquired about the whereabouts of Dr. Shamim which was not at all the business of the appellant. If Dr. Shamim was a Bangalee and was present in Bangladesh, he may not have occupied, managed or supervised the suit property in person for many reasons, but there is no earthly reason why he did not contest the money suit filed by Rupali Bank, why he did not resist the auction sale of hes Valuable suit property and why, finding Radio Bangladesh to be in possession of his property, he did not make any effort to release his property from the possession of the Government. Man may lie, but circumstances do not and in the circumstances of the case it appears to us that bah the Courts below turned a blind eye to the admitted circumstances of the case and were swayed by the verbal assertions of the auction-purchaser's witnesses without weighing them with the attendant circumstance of the case and without probing the evidentiary value of their statements when the circumstances themselves speak a volume against their assertions. 17. The High Court Division made much of the tact that the Government did not form any opinion as to whether the suit property was an abandoned property or not, little caring to notice that in the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs. M/s. Speedbird Navigation Co. 30 DLR (SC) 101, this Division held, "No doubt the determination is only an ascertainment of fact constituting a property an abandoned property, and on such preliminary ascertainment of fact the law takes effect of it own force from 28.2.72, the date the order came into force". While allotting the suit property to Radio Bangladesh on 11.7.72 the Government already formed an opinion that the suit property was an abandoned property and it is the case of the appellant that it was "allotted" as an abandoned house for office accommodation of the Director-General, Radio Bangladesh. There is no evidence that Government treated Radio Bangladesh as an unauthorised possessor and demanded arrear rent. Radio Bangladesh was a regular allotee of the Government of an abandoned property since July, 1972. All these facts stare in the face and we have no hesitation in finding that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that there was no formation of opinion by the Government that the suit property was an abandoned property. 18. The suit property eminently answers the definition of abandoned property in Article 2(1) of President's Order No. 16 of 1972 in that the circumstances of the case sleraly prove that Dr. Shamim was not present in Bangladesh, his where-abouts were not known and he ceased to occupy supervise or manage the property in person. The two Courts below erred in law in holding that the suit property is not an abandoned property. 19. This Division has held in the case of Gannyson vs. Sonali Bank, 36 DLR (AD) 146, that once a property vests in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 no legal proceedings can be taken against such property. The money decree obtained by Rupali Bank against Dr. Shamim, the execution thereof and the auction sale of the suit property are all void and will not divest the Government of its title to the suit property and the auction-purchaser has acquired no title to the same by his auction purchase. 20. With regard to CP No.15 of 1994 Mr. TH Khan submits that it is time-barred by 126 days. 21. Wee find from the records that CP No. 14 of 1994 from which CA No. 14 of 1994 arises was filed on 13.1.94 within time and CP No. 47 of 1994 out of which CA No. 15 of 1994 arises was filed on 5.2.94 and the office note says that it was filed within time. While in CP No. 14 of 1994 the certified copies of the judgments of the High Court Division and the trial Court were filed in CP No. 47 of 1994 those were not filed and on 5.2.94 an application was filed by the appellant for dispensing with the filing of certified copies in that particular petition, the parties and judgments being the same in the other Civil Petition. Owing to some lapses of the office this application was not put up before the learned Judge in Chamber for orders. We have no hesitation in holding that had the application been put up before the learned Judge in Chamber it would have been allowed consistent with the practice and procedure of this Court. CA No. 15 of 1994 is time-barred for purely technical and ministerial reasons. The appellant is not guilty of any latches. We therefore condone the delay in filing Ck No. 15 of 1994. Both the appeals are therefore allowed without any order as to costs. Title Suit No. 339 of 1981 is dismissed and Title suit No. 69 of 1981 is decreed without costs. End.
