full_judgment: Mustafa Kamal J : This appeal by leave of the plaintiff appellant is from the judgment and order dated 9-6-94 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1350 of 1993 making the Rule absolute and setting aside judgment dated 6-2-93 passed by the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge Sylhet allowing an amendment of the plaint in Title Suit No. 415/84 of the said Court. 2. In the leave petition the appellant alleged that he instituted Title Suit No. 214 of 1977 (re-numbered as Title Suit No. 415 of 1984) in the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet for specific performance of contract against Habiba Banu (since deceased) and respondent Nos. 1-6 as defendants on the allegations inter alia that the defendants entered into a contract with the appellant on 21-4-76 for sale of 1.09 acre of land for a consideration of Taka 2,75,143.00 by executing a bainapatra on that date and receiving Taka 50,000.00 as advance. The agreement was that the vendors would execute and register deeds of sale on receipt of the balance of consideration money by different deeds either in favour of the appellant or in favour of his nominees who are respondent Nos.7-19 in this appeal. The appellant and respondent Nos. 7-19 obtained possession of the land under contract and after dividing the said land amicably amongst themselves the appellant kept for himself three plots measuring about 39 decimals and a common pathway of about 0.06 acres of land described in Schedule-IV of the plaint which is the suit land. Respondent Nos. 1-6 and Habiba Banu executed and registered 10 different kabalas in respect of 0.64 acres of land in favour of the nominees of the appellant on receipt of Taka 2,74,500.00 out of Taka 2,75,143.00 and only Taka 643.00 remained the balance to be paid to the vendors. When the appellant demanded execution and registration of a Kabala in his favour in respect of the remaining 0.45 acres of land deceased Habiba Banu demanded Taka 50,000.(X) more on the plea of increase in the value of land. After tiling the suit the appellant obtained an order of injunction against defendant Nos. 1-7 restraining them from interfering with the possession of the appellant in the suit land. 3. The deceased defendant Habiba Banu and respondent Nos. 1 and 2 filing written statements contended that the appellant having not performed his part of the contract within the time stipulated and time being of the essence of the contract was not entitled to specific performance of contract. The bainapatra was collusively amended by the appellant by changing two pages. 1.07 acre of land was stipulated to be sold but by collusively changing the bainapatra the area to be sold was shown as 1.09 acre. The appellant trespassed into the suit land and the suit was false. 4 . In June, 1986 both sides adduced evidence at the trial of the suit. But at the time of argument the defendants lawyer pointed out that summons and notices were not served upon defendant No. 5, Khalequzzaman who was in Dhaka Central Jail at the relevant time. The appellant filed an application praying for issuance of a fresh summons upon defendant No. 5. All the defendants arc members of the same family and there is a community of interest between them. The trial Court by order dated 24-6-86 rejected the application against which the appellant preferred Civil Revision No. 131 of 1986 in the Sylhet Bench of the High Court Division and obtained a Rule and stay of further proceedings of the suit. 5. During the pendency of the said civil revisional case, taking advantage of the absence of the appellant's attorney who went to perform Hajj the defendants on 12-8-86 ousted the chowkidar of the appellant from the suit land, took possession thereof and opened a poultry farm in one of the suit plots. The appellant's attorney on return from Hajj filed a miscellaneous case for violation of injunction. Rule in the said Civil Revision No. 131of 1986 was discharged on 26-11-90 with the observation that under Order IX, rule 6(2) there is a provision in the Code of Civil Procedure to file a fresh suit against a defendant on whom summons and notices could not be served. After disposal of the civil revision case it was found that in one of the suit lands one Md. Mohsin and his wife Rabeya Begum were making preparation for construction of a building. The appellant obtained certified copies of documents executed by Habiba Banu and other defendants in favour of the said Mohsin and Rabeya Begum and their three minor sons in 1987 and in favour of one Abdur Rahim and his wife and son in 1989. 6. On 7-2-91 the appellant then filed Title Suit No. 40 of 1991 against defendant No. 5 Khalequzzaman of Title Suit No.415 of 1984 for specific performance of contract, recovery of possession and injunction, impleading the subsequent purchasers of the suit land as defendant Nos. 2-11 and the defendants of the earlier suit as pro-forma defendants. The suit was filed before the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet but as at the relevant time the pecuniary jurisdiction of the Senior Assistant Judge was increased to Taka 1 lakh the plaint was returned and the appellant had to refile the suit in the court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Sylhet. He obtained an order of status quo in respect of the said land against the said Md. Mohsin and others. 7. On 7-4-91 the appellant filed the instant application for amendment of the plaint of the earlier Title Suit No. 415 of 1984 seeking to implead the subsequent purchasers as defendants and seeking to replace the prayer for confirmation of possession of the suit land with a prayer for recovery of possession of the suit land from all the original defendants and subsequent purchasers of the suit land. In the application for amendment of the plaint all the events that took place after the evidence was adduced at the trial of the suit in June, 1986 were stated and sought to be incorporated in the body of the plaint. The appellant also filed an application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the learned District Judge, Sylhet for transfer of the later suit, namely, Title Suit No. 40 of 1991, from the Court of Senior Assistant Judge to the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet and for analogous hearing of the two title suits, which gave rise to Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 1991 registering which the learned District Judge called for the records of both the suits and upon the prayer of the appellant passed an order of temporary injunction restraining the subsequent purchasers from proceeding with the construction work, which order of temporary injunction was challenged by the subsequent purchasers in the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.1828 of 1991 in which the Rule was ultimately discharged. By Judgement and order dated 30-1-92 in Miscellaneous Case No. 17 of 1991 the learned District Judge allowed transfer of the subsequent title suit to the 2nd Court of learned Subordinate Judge and left the matter of analogous hearing to be decided by the learned Subordinate Judge himself. On transfer to the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge Title Suit No. 40 of 1991 was re-numbered as Title Suit No. 23 of 1992. The subsequent purchaser Md. Mohsin challenged the learned District Judge's order dated 30-1-92 in Miscellaneous Case No.17 of 1991 by preferring Civil Revision No.496 of 1992 in the High Court Division and obtained a Rule and stay of operation of the impugned judgment and order of the learned District Judge. By judgment and order dated 8-11-92 a Division Bench of the High Court Division discharged the Rule observing that both the suits be tried separately. 8. After disposal of Civil Revision No. 496 of 1992 the appellant's application for amendment of the plaint dated 7-4-91 came up for hearing. No written objection was filed by the defendant-respondents and after hearing both sides the application was allowed without giving any reason by the learned Subordinate Judge by order dated 6-2-93 against which some of the respondents preferred Civil Revision No. 1350 of 1993 in the High Court Division and obtained a Rule. By the impugned judgment and order the learned Judges of the High Court Division disallowed the amendment of plaint on the ground that the facts of a later suit cannot be incorporated in the pleadings of an earlier suit and that the amendment sought for is mala fide. 9. Leave was granted to consider the appellant's submission that the High Court Division erred in law in coming to the aforesaid findings without paying regard to the facts, circumstances and situations under which the appellant had to file the application for amendment of plaint in the earlier suit. The appellant had the right to seek an amendment of plaint for incorporation of events and situations that developed and transpired after the filing of the suit, even if the appellant had not filed any subsequent suit. The proposed amendment has not in any way changed the character of either the suit or the plaint. In the absence of the amendment the appellant's success in any of the two suits will be illusory and infructuous, giving him no benefits. He has thus been rendered by the impugned judgment remedyless. 10. Mr. Fazlul Haque, learned Advocate appearing with the leave of the Court for the plaintiff-appellant, submits that the learned Judges of the High Court Division did not dispute the well-established proposition of law that events and developments evolved and transpired after the filing of the suit may be incorporated by way of amendment of the plaint, but distinguished the present case on the ground that the appellant sought to amend the plaint of Title Suit No.415 of 1984 by bringing certain facts, materials and prayers of a later suit, namely, Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge, Sylhet, The High Court Division observed that there is no decision in which it has been held that the facts and prayers of a pending suit may be incorporated in the pleadings and prayers of another pending suit by way of amendment. Mr. Fazlul Huque submits that the position taken by the High Court Division is in an absolute turning over of the eyes on the nature and purposes of the two suits and the inextricable connection between them. 11. Dr. Ahmed Hossain, learned Advocate for respondent Nos. 1 and 2, could not point out from the impugned judgment that the connection between the two title suits was at all considered by the High Court Division. 12. It was absolutely under compulsion that the appellant had to file the subsequent Title Suit No. 23 of 1992 against defendant No. 5 of Title Suit No. 415 of 1984 and the subsequent purchasers claiming specific performance of contract and recovery of possession from them. The subsequent suit filed against defendant No. 5 is subject to the law of limitation and it is a risk which the appellant was driven to undertake, had it not been for the fact that the learned Subordinate Judge rejected his petition for issuance of a fresh summons against the said defendant. If the appellant was not thus driven to file the subsequent suit, he was entitled under the law to incorporate in his first suit by way of amendment of plaint all the subsequent events and developments that took place after June 1986. He also could have added the subsequent purchasers as defendants and could have substituted his prayer for confirmation of possession with a prayer for recovery of possession as it is his allegation that he was dispossessed during the pendency of the earlier suit. It would not have changed the nature and character of either the plaint or the suit. In the event of his success in the earlier suit his remedy would have been complete and effective. The filing of the subsequent suit is an act of compulsion and not of choice. The appellant still retains the full right to obtain complete relief in the earlier title suit by incorporating facts and prayers which arose out of subsequent events, no matter whether those facts and prayers were incorporated in the subsequent suit. The learned Judges of the High Court Division appeared to have conveniently overlooked that the two Suits are inextricably linked and are not suits of different nature fought against stranger, the earlier suit on a different cause of action and upon seeking prayers of a different nature, so that one suit is so different from the other that the facts of one cannot be incorporated into the other by way of amendment. The High Court Division should have realised that if the impugned judgment stands the appellant in the event of his success in the earlier suit will not be able to obtain an effective decree at all. It will be for all purposes an infructuous decree. In the event of his success in the subsequent suit as well the plaintiff will get an incomplete decree because the original defendants who were parties to the contract of sale will not be signatories to a sale deed in the later suit as no relief was claimed against them, they being mere proforma-defendants in the latter suit. In either case, if the impugned judgment stands, the plaintiff will be virtually without any remedy. 13. We therefore, are of the opinion that the High Court Division completely failed to apply its mind as to the nature and connection between the two suits and had gone to an unnecessarily lengthy extreme to separate the earlier suit from the later to deny the appellant a legitimate amendment which to the learned Subordinate Judge appeared to be so rightly logical and consequential that he readily acceded to the prayer without wasting any words. It is significant that the defendants did not file any written objection. 14. The High Court Division disallowed the amendment also on the ground of mala fide. It noticed that after the amendment was allowed by the trial Court the appellant was trying to withdraw the later suit. It also found that the appellant tried hard to get an analogous trial of the two suits, but since the High Court Division in an earlier civil revisional case observed that the cases should be tried separately, the proposed amendment was concocted as a device to circumvent that observation rendering the application as mala fide. 15. Again, the said finding is a result of an abject failure of the High Court Division to understand and comprehend the nature and connection of the two suits. The later suit, as we have already noticed, is an involuntary one thrust upon the appellant because of a technical failure to effect service of summons and notices upon defendant No.5. The filing of the second suit is good enough punishment for the plaintiff for his lapses in the earlier suit, but to disallow him to make his earlier suit a complete one with all parties present, all facts stated and all relevant claims made, is to punish him altogether for filing any suit at all against the respondents. We note with dismay that instead of furthering the cause of justice by allowing the plaintiff-appellant a full opportunity to place his case against all the parties involved by stating all the facts that he wants to allege against them and by seeking all possible remedies against them, the High Court Division has given a queer look at the plaintiff and has found him lacking in bona fide in whatever he docs. After all, he is seeking full justice from a Court of law and he wants to bring all the parties involved in the original and subsequent transactions. Why should anyone find a malafide motive in trying to do just that is beyond our comprehension. It is for the plaintiff-appellant to do whatever he likes with the later suit. The direction to hold separate trial does not mean that the plaintiff-appellant must pursue the second suit or else his first suit will be strictly limited within its original frame. The plaintiff as the arbitrates of his suits has the liberty to pursue or not to pursue any one of the two suits. And the two suits being inextricably linked together can be amended according as the plaintiff wishes to lay stress on either the first suit or the second suit, having regard to the fact that he is obliged to pursue the two suits basically for the same remedy. 16. We do not think therefore that the High Court Division made a correct approach to this simple problem and we further notice with dismay that it made a mountain out of a molehill in writing an unnecessarily lengthy judgment on such a simple matter. The appeal is allowed with costs. The impugned judgment and order arc set aside and the order dated 6-2-93 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in Title Suit No. 415 of 1984 is restored. End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 97 of 1988 (Barisal)
 Civil Revision No. 2861 of 1991 (Dhaka)
lawyer:
Md Shahidul Haque, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
No one ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Sonali Bank ------ Petitioner
vs.
Mozaffor Hossain  ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Feeling aggrieved by a judgment and order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, restoring a suit to its file and number, on allowing Miscellaneous Case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the plaintiff approached  this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon a Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 23-3-1988 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Barisal, in Miscellaneous Case No. 66 of 1983 should not be set aside. 

2. The only question that falls for determination in this Rule is whether the defendant opposite party had sufficient cause for non-appearance when the suit was called on for hearing and whether the impugned judgment and order of restoration of the suit on setting aside the ex parte decree was well-founded on law within the meaning of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure 

3. For the purpose of answering to the said question, the factual canvass of the matter may be adverted to which is set out below: The petitioner, Sonali Bank, as plaintiff on 2-2-1978 instituted a suit being Money Suit No.3 of 1978 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal against the defendant for realisation of Taka 41,487.20 with cost and interest till realisation of the entire amount due under cash credit account accrued by mortgage along with other two accounts. Notice of the suit had been duly served upon the defendant but with an ulterior motive, the defendant did not appear in the suit in time. The suit was fixed on 8-9-1987 for ex parte disposal. On that date, the defendant filed a petition praying for time for filing written statement. Time was allowed and on 15-11-1978 was fixed for submitting written statement by the defendant. The defendant, with malafide intention, without filing written statement, on 15-11.1978 by way of an application, prayed for direction upon the plaintiff for production of certain documents mentioned in the said petition. The defendant also filed another application praying for the time for submitting written statement. The plaintiff on 22-11-1978 produced documents for inspection by the defendant but defendant did not file written statement. The learned Subordinate Judge rejected the petition of the defendant for filing written statement and again fixed 18-12-1978 for ex parte disposal. The defendant, ultimately, on 18-12-1978 filed written statement admitting taking of cash credit advance from Bank but denied his liability of interest. 

4. The suit was fixed on 4-7-1979 for peremptory hearing. The defendant took adjournment on the ground of illness and 11-9-1979 was fixed for peremptory hearing. On 11-9-1979, defendant filed an application for adjournment for the purpose of realising plaintiffs claim on amicable settlement. Adjournment was allowed till 2-1-1981. The defendant in that way took adjournments on 20 dates, all fixed for peremptory hearing. Lastly, 31-5-1983 was fixed for peremptory hearing. On that date also, the defendant prayed for adjournment for peremptory on the plea of coming to an amicable settlement with the plaintiff-Bank. The learned Subordinate Judge rejected the prayer of the defendant and asked both the plaintiff and the defendant to get ready for hearing. The plaintiff was present in the Court for hearing but the defendant was found absent on repeated calls. The suit was taken up for ex parte disposal. But, as the Court's hour was over, 13-6-1983 was fixed for ex parte disposal. On 13-6-1983 plaintiff filed hazira but the defendant did not take any step and was found absent on repeated calls. The suit was taken for ex parte disposal. Mr Shah Alam Khan an Officer of the plaintiff-Bank was examined as PW 1 in support of the plaintiff’s case. Documents were marked as Exhibits. 31-7-1983 was fixed for order. On 31-7-1983, the suit was decreed ex parte and money decree for Taka 41,487.20 had been awarded in favour of the plaintiff-Bank. 

5. The defendant, thereafter, on 30-8-1993 filed an application being numbered as Miscellaneous Case No.66 of 1983 under the provisions of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, for restoration of the suit to its file and number, on setting aside the ex parte decree, taking the ground that final decision with respect to the claim of the plaintiff-Bank having not been reached, he was compelled to file application for adjournment of the peremptory hearings and he sustained loss by the ex parte decree. 

6. The plaintiff-Bank resisted the Miscellaneous Case by filing written objection denying all the allegations made in the Miscellaneous Case and took the stand that the defendant, with a malafide motive, to cause delay of the disposal of the suit and also, to cause unnecessary harassment to the Bank, took adjournments after adjournments on false pleas. Further stand taken is that no case had been made out by the defendant that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the suit was taken up for hearing. It was also pleaded that by the ex parte decree, the defendant did not sustain any loss and injury. 

7. The learned Subordinate Judge by the impugned judgment and order dated 23-3-1988 allowed the Miscellaneous Case on contest and restored the suit to its file and number on setting aside the ex parte decree passed on 31-7-1983. 

8. The plaintiff-Bank challenged the aforesaid judgment and order before this Court in an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule. 

9. The plaintiff-petitioner is represented by the learned Advocate Mr Shahidul Haque. The defendant opposite party, though, filed power, did not contest the Rule at the time of hearing of the same. 

10. Mr Md Shahidul Haque, in support of the Rule, submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge committed a substantial error in the decision in setting aside the ex parte decree without being satisfied as to the sufficiency of cause which prevented the defendant from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. In developing argument, the learned Advocate contended that neither the petition under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor the evidence of the defendant did disclose any cause of action as contemplated under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code and the learned Subordinate Judge committed a grave error in the decision in restoring the suit to its file and number. 

11. The next contention raised from the side of the plaintiff-petitioner is that the defendant was required to ventilate the grievance of non- consideration of the ground taken in the application for adjournment dated 31-5-1983 by way of a Civil Revisional application before the High Court Division and he was not allowed to challenge the said order under the provisions of Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

12. Before I advert to the contentions raised from the side of the petitioner, it will be appropriate to quote the relevant provision of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure which reads as follows: "13-In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant, he may apply to the Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside; and if he satisfies the Court that the summons was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called for hearing, the Court shall make an order setting aside the decree as against him upon such terms as to costs, payment into Court or otherwise as it thinks fit, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit; Provided that where the decree is of such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendants only it may be set aside as against all or any of the other defendants also." 

13. From a reading of the above provisions, it is manifested that an ex parte decree can be set aside on two grounds, (i) that the summons was not duly served, or (ii) that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. The second one is relevant for the present purpose. 

14. Keeping in view of the above provisions, I am now to see whether the defendant could prove by legal evidence that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing. 

15. The case before me got an unfortunate carrier of adjournments taken by the defendant. The record of the case had not been called for at the time of issuance of Rule. Learned Advocate for the petitioner has placed before me the certified copies of the order sheet starting from the date of registration of the plaint till the date of ex parte decree awarded in favour of the plaintiff-Bank. It appears that the plaint was registered on 2-2-1978. The defendant did not appear in the suit in spite of proper service of notice upon him. The Court, ultimately, fixed 19-8-1978 for ex parte disposal. On that date, the defendant appeared and filed a petition for time for filing written statement. The Court allowed the defendant's prayer for time with cost of Taka 50.00 on condition of filing written statement within 15-11-1978. On15-11-1978, the defendant did not file written statement and, thus, violated the condition imposed upon him by the Court in its order dated 8-9-1978. The defendant filed a petition for time for filing written statement and also, filed another application under Order XI rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for a direction upon the plaintiff to file basic documents in Court as mentioned in the petition. The Court on the same date ie 15-11-1978 directed the plaintiff to file basic documents. The Court, by the same order, directed the defendant to file written statement by 4-12-1978. The order of the Court was to the effect" the defendant must file WS by 4-12-1978." On 4-12-1978, the defendant, instead of filing written statement, filed an application praying for time for filing written statement, The Court rejected the said prayer and once again, fixed 18-12-1978 for ex parte disposal. On 18-12-1978, the defendant filed written statement which was accepted by the Court. The suit was fixed for peremptory hearing on 4-7-1979. On 4-7-1979, plaintiff filed hazira and the defendant filed an application praying for adjournment of peremptory hearing. The prayer for adjournment was allowed with cost of Taka 30.00 CP. The learned Advocate for the defendant undertook not to take further time. The order dated 4-7-1979 is extracted thus: "18/4- 7 -79 plff. files hazira. Deft. files a petition praying for adjournment of P. hearing, copy served. The Advocate for the Deft.  undertakes not to take further time. Heard both sides. The prayer is allowed with cost of Taka 30.00 CP Toll-9-79 for P hearing. Sd/" Illegible, SJ 

16. Thereafter, the dates, 11-9-79, 25-2-80, 8-4-1980, 24-6-80, 17-12-80, 18-2-81, 29-4-81,• 3-7-81, 8-9-81, 11-12-81, 26-2-82, 23-4-82, 22-6-82,20-8-82,11-1-83,23-3-83 and 31-5-83 had been fixed for peremptory hearing. In all those dates, defendant sought for adjournment for peremptory hearing, sometimes on the ground of amicable settlement to be reached between the plaintiff-Bank and the defendant and sometimes on other grounds. 

17. On 31-5-1983, plaintiff filed hazira. The defendant by way of an application prayed for an adjournment taking the ground of amicable settlement between the defendant and the plaintiff- Bank. The learned Subordinate Judge rejected the same as being harassing and directed the parties to be ready for hearing at once. The plaintiff was present in the Court for the purpose of peremptory hearing but the defendant did not take any step and he was found absent in the Court. The suit was, thereafter, taken up for ex parte disposal. The Court's time having been over, 13-6-1983 was fixed for ex parte disposal. On 13-6-1983, plaintiff filed hazira but the defendant did not take any step and was found absent on repeated calls. The suit was taken up for ex parte disposal. Mr. Shah Alam Khan, an officer of the plaintiff-Bank was examined as PW 1 Documents had been also marked as Exhibits. Thereafter, 31.7.1983 was fixed for order. On 31.7.1983, the suit was decreed ex parte with cost and money decree of Taka 41,487.20 had been awarded in favour of the plaintiff-Bank. 

18. It is significant to note, that on 31-5-1983 defendant's prayer for adjournment was rejected and both the plaintiff and the defendant were directed by the Court to get ready at once but the defendant, neither did take any further step, nor did care to be present in the Court. The Court's time having been over, ex parte hearing of the suit could not be taken up and13-6-1983 was fixed for ex parte disposal. On 13-6-1983 also, the defendant did not take any step and remained absent from the Court and he was found absent on repeated calls. The defendant, though, was required to take information of the fate of the suit, remained quite unconcerned with the result of the suit. Lastly, on 31-7-1983 when ex parte decree was passed, the defendant had also chosen to be absent in the Court. This conduct of the defendant must not be over looked. 

19; From all the materials, events, facts, circumstances and the conduct of the defendant it became evidently clear that all the efforts of the defendant were directed to cause deliberate delay in disposal of the suit and to cause unnecessary harassment to the plaintiff-Bank, the object being  the non-payment of Bank money and the defendant having failed to get further adjournment, deliberately absented himself from the Court and allowed the suit to be decreed ex parte against him. 

20. Let me now turn back to the pertinent question as to the sufficiency of cause for non-appearance on the part of the defendant in the suit when it was called on for hearing. In the application under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code, it is stated that the final decision having not been reached by the plaintiff-Bank with respect to amicable settlement, the defendant was compelled to file an application for adjournment of peremptory hearing. It has, further, been stated that the Court rejected the said application and decreed the suit ex parte on 31-7-83. From the statements made in the application, it does not, at all, appear that the defendant could make out a case that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was called on for hearing within the meaning of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code. The defendant Md Mozaffar Hossain as PW 1 gave evidence that the prayer for remission of interest and the payment of loan money on installment, having been under consideration of the plaintiff-Bank, he took adjournments on different dates and lastly, on 31-7-83 he filed an application for adjournment on the same ground and the Court rejected the prayer and awarded decree in favour of the plaintiff and by the decree, he sustained loss. By this evidence also, the defendant could not make out a case of sufficient cause as contemplated under part II of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code. 

21. In order to come under the purview of the Second Part of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code, the defendant was to satisfy the Court that there was sufficient cause for his non-appearance on the date when the suit was actually called on for hearing and when the evidence of the plaintiff was recorded. For setting aside ex parte decree, the defendant had to show cause for his absence on the date of actual ex parte hearing. In the instant case, 13-5-1983 was fixed for ex parte disposal of the suit but the suit was not disposed of ex parte on that date. The suit was taken up for ex parte disposal on 13-6-1983 and the evidence of the plaintiff-Bank was recorded and documents produced in support of the claim had been exhibited. Thus, from the legal point of view, 13-6-1983 was the actual date for ex parte disposal of the suit. The defendant did not assign any reason, whatsoever, for his non-appearance on 13.6.1983 when the suit was actually taken up for ex parte hearing. The defendant having not made out a case that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing in the Court on 13-6-1983, he could not come for setting aside the ex parte decree showing cause for his non-appearance on 31-5-1983. The defendant, therefore, failed to make out a case for restoration of the suit on setting aside the ex parte decree as contemplated under the provisions of law contained in Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

22. Let me now see how far the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in restoring the suit to its file and number on setting aside the ex parte decree. 

23. On perusal of the impugned judgment, it seems that in deciding the miscellaneous case, the learned Subordinate Judge did not keep in mind the provisions of Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and misdirected himself in his approach on the matter. The learned Subordinate Judge held that as because the learned Lawyer for the plaintiff, on the application for adjournment, received copy without prejudice, so it was proved that the subject matter of the application for time filed by the defendant was correct and the plaintiff had knowledge of that. The learned Judge further held that in view of the circumstances, the application for adjournment filed by the defendant was required to be granted. The learned Subordinate Judge, thus, appears to have missed the true import of the provisions of law embodied in Order 9 rule 13 of the Code. Moreover the Court did not at all notice that the defendant on the plea of amicable settlement took 18 (eighteen) adjournments for peremptory hearing as a part of his delaying tactic. From the facts, materials and circumstances of the case, it became clear that the defendant had chosen to non-co-operate with the Court. Having adopted such a stand towards the Court, the defendant got no right to ask its indulgence. The Court also, failed to consider the conduct of the defendant who was admittedly a defaulter for non-payment of loan money due to the plaintiff-Bank. The impugned judgment was, therefore, not warranted by law and interference, hence, is called for in the exercise of power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

24. In view of the discussion made herein-above, I am of this considered view that the Rule got merit and the same, thus, succeeds. 

25. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 23-3-1983 passed in Miscellaneous Case No.66 of 1983 arising out of Money Suit No.3 of 1978 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Barisal is set aside and the ex parte decree dated 30- 7 -1983 is maintained. 

Order of stay stands vacated. 

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani J: This appeal by the substituted plaintiffs from a decree dismissing their suit for mesne profits.

2. At the outset Mr. Moinul Huq, learned Advocate for some of the defendants respondents, placed his previously filed affidavits with annexures wherein it has been stated that the defendant No. 3 Delowar Hossain Khan died on 18.7.82 and that defendant No. 2 Motahar Hossain Khan died on 18.2.78 whereas the suit was decreed on 20.1.87 and, as such, the suit abated as a whole.

3. In reply Mr. MI Faruqui submits that those defendants did not contest the suit and so substitutions of their respective heirs were not necessary in view of Order 22 rule 4(4) of Civil Procedure Code.

<u>4. Mr. Faruqui is not correct. Law requires that if a party to the suit dies, then either an application for substituting his or her heirs or an application for seeking exemption in accordance with Order 22 rule 4(4) of Civil Procedure Code shall have to be filed within the statutory period of 90 days. A plaintiff cannot get the exemption automatically without filing an application or a court cannot exercise the power of exemption after suit has abated. This is also the view of the Calcutta High Court in AIR 1975 (Cal) 12.</u>

<u>We however, hold that the suit abated only as against the defendant Nos. 2 and 3. We also find that both the deceased defendants filed separate written statements jointly with some others.</u>

5. 1.69 acre of land situated within Mouza Kakrail city of Dhaka, is the subject matter. Plaint case is that Oriental Development and Construction Ltd. acquired title to this land. In 1951 four persons Awlad Hossain Khan, Md. Fazlul Karim, Syed Abdul Hamid and Amina Khatun trespassed into this land, constructed some pucca and kutcha structures and thereby dispossessed the said owner who instituted Title Suit No.10 of 1952 in the 3rd. Court of Sub-Ordinate Judge, Dhaka, for khas possession on declaration of title against the said alleged trespassers.

6. During the pendency of the suit two persons Hamidul Huq Chowdhury and Rahimullah Chowdury purchased this land and got themselves added as co-plaintiffs in the said suit. Both the co-plaintiffs and the defendants excepting Amina Khatun died and their respective heirs have been pursuing the litigations.

7. The co-plaintiffs filed a money suit on 8.4.61 ultimately registered as Money Suit No. 22 of 1986 on transfer to the 3rd Court of Sub-Ordinate Judge, Dhaka for the following reliefs:

a) That a declaration may he made that the plaintiffs are entitled to get the mesne profit against the defendant Nos. 1-26 personally and as representatives-in-interest of their respective predecessors jointly and severally.

b) That an enquiry may be made as to the amount of mesne profits which the plaintiffs are entitled to get from the principal defendants in respect of the suit properties described in the plaint for the period of 3 years prior to the institution of the suit and also for the period from the date of institution of the suit up to the date of delivery of possession of the suit land and that for the purpose of enquiry a Commissioner may be appointed or the court may be pleased to make enquiry itself.

c) That a decree may be passed for the amount found due to the plaintiffs upon such enquiry against the defendant Nos. 1-26 jointly or severally on receipt of additional court fee, if necessary.

d)	That a decree for cost of the suit.

e)	That a decree for such other relief or reliefs as the Hon'ble Court may deem fit and proper in favour of the plaintiffs.

8. In this money suit defendant Nos. 1 to 14 are the heirs of aforesaid Awalad Hossain Khan, defendant Nos. 16 to 22 are the heirs of aforesaid Md. Fazlul Karim and defendant Nos. 23 to 26 are the heirs of aforesaid Syed Abdul Hamid. Amina Khatun is defendant No. 1.

9. Ultimately the title suit was decreed on 28.8.62. The decree was then unsuccessfully challenged in the then Dhaka High Court and in the Supreme Court ending the matter finally on 12.6.69.

10. The appellants filed an application for accepting certain papers as additional evidence. This Division passed order on 7.8.89 to the effect that this application would be considered at the time of hearing of the appeal. Proposed additional evidence are the certified copies of the order sheet of title execution case No. 8 of 1963, advocate commissioners report in the execution case, and two applications of the plaintiff’s decree holders and a written objection by some of the judgment debtors filed in the execution case. We have considered the application and find that we require the first two papers, order sheet and the report, to enable us to pronounce judgment and as such we allow the prayer for additional evidence in respect of the said two papers which are respectively annexure-A' and 'B' to the application for additional evidence and reject the prayer in respect of the others. From said annexure 'A' it appears that the decree passed in the title suit was put into execution vide title Execution Case No.8 of 1963. It appears from annexure-B' that the learned Advocate Commissioner on 6.12.81 delivered the possession to the decree holders appellants of the suit land except the entire land of CS plot Nos. 117 and 18 and part of CS Plot No. 116 lying south of the main road. Consequently the learned advocate commissioners again went to the decretal land when the decree holders were given possession of entire CS Plot No. 118 and part of CS plot No.116 after removing minor structures thereon. Thereafter the learned Advocate Commissioner went to the decretal land with police force on 1.5.83. One Abdul Mannan was then living with his family in a tin shed with pucca walls on CS Plot No. 117. Structures under the possession of Abdul Mannan were removed and the decree holders were given possession thereof. The learned Advocate Commissioner on measurement fixed the decretal land out of CS plot No. 116 and delivered possession thereof by posting wooden pegs. But the decree holders were not satisfied and we may presume that due to this the execution case has not yet been disposed of.

11. It must be noticed that the money suit was filed during the pendency of the title suit and, as such, a pertinent question will be whether the money suit was maintainable for mesne profits in respect of the land when previous suit for possession in respect thereof was pending, However the money suit was taken up for peremptory hearing on 15.6.86, the parties contested the same and ultimately the suit was dismissed by the judgment and decree dated 20.1.87.

12. This question was never raised obviously in view of the well settled principle that a successful plaintiff in a suit for possession can bring a suit for mesne profits, as the causes of action for the suits are different. But this is not the case here. In the title suit the plaintiffs at any stage could have prayed for mesne profits already accrued prior to the institution of the suit and that from the institution of the suit until the possession was delivered to them and in that case the trial Court could have passed a decree for mesne profits in accordance with Order 20 rule 12 of Civil Procedure Code.

13. Perhaps sensing this anomaly, Mr. MI Faruqui, the learned Advocate for the appellants, submits that since that suit for possessing was decreed in favour of the plaintiffs and possession of the suit land was delivered to the plaintiffs through Court so nothing remained for the plaintiffs to prove in this suit for mesne profits and the trial Court was found to pass a preliminary decree in accordance with Order 20 rule 12 of Civil Procedure Code and then it ought to have been the function of the Commissioner appointed by the Court to ascertain the mesne profits as defined in section 2(12) of Civil Procedure Code.

14. On the other hand, Mr. Moinul Huq, the learned leading Advocate for the respondents, submits that in an independent suit for mesne profits there is no question of passing a preliminary decree and the Court shall have to pass a final decree either it allows or dismisses the suit on the basis of the evidence on record. Then Mr. Huq submits that in this suit it is impossible to pass a decree for the court on the basis of the evidence on record. As we like to answer the first point first together with our self-query as to maintainability of the suit itself, we like to narrate and consider Mr. Huq's second point later on.

<u>15. Mr. MI Faruqui, we find, is not correct in his submissions if we simply look into the opening sentence of Order 20 rule 12 of Civil Procedure Code which reads, where a suit is for the recovery of possession of immovable property and for rent for mesne profit. The word "and" is underlined by us for emphasis. This provision is not for a suit for mesne profits simpliciter. True after the disposal of his suit for possession, a right to claim of mesne profits accrues to the successful plaintiff, but he cannot have cause of action to pursue a suit for mesne profits simultaneously with his previous suit for possession as in that case cause of action for both the suits are his dispossession and that is why provision for passing a preliminary decree of necessity has been provided for such a suit both for possession and mesne profits keeping the relief for mesne profits to be decided after the court first decides the relief for possession on merit. In case the court dismisses a suit for possession, then determination of mesne profits becomes useless, but if the court decrees the suit then a preliminary decree is required to be passed for mesne profits. But in a suit for mesne profits after the disposal of the suit the issue before the court is only what will be the quantum of mesne profits. It has been held in 66 CWN 692 that Order 20 rule 12 of Civil Procedure Code is merely an enabling provision, permitting the Court in a suit for possession, to pass also on the plaintiffs prayer, if he So chooses, a decree for past and future mesne profits and this rule has no manner of application in a suit only for mesne profits.</u>

<u>16. We, therefore, hold that the plaintiffs suit for mesne profits instituted separately during the pendency of their previous suit for possession was not maintainable and ought to have been dismissed on this count. We further hold that provisions of Order 20 rule 12 of Civil Procedure Code do not apply to a suit for mesne profits simpliciter and, as such, both the parties in such a suit are required to adduce evidence, for and against, as to quantum of claim and the Court is required to determine the issue finally on the basis of the evidence on record.</u>

17. We now like to consider the second point of Mr. Moinul Huq. According to Mr. Huq, the plaintiffs have given go bye to their case in the plaint by introducing different story at the time of trial through their only witness, PW 1 SM Yunus. Some of the statements of the PW 1 as pointed out by Mr. Huq are as follows:

বিবাদীগণ বে-আইনীভাবে নালিশী ভূমিতে দখলকার ছিলেন এবং এখনও কতকাংশে বে-আইনীভাবে দখলকার আছেন। বাদীগণ নালিশী সম্পত্তির দখল পান ১৯৫৩/১৯৫৪ সালে বাকী অংশ বিবাদীগণের দখলে এবং বাকী অংশ বাদীর দখলে।

18. Mr. Huq then reads out certain statements of DW 1 and DW 2 which were not challenged in the cross-examination by the plaintiffs. They are as follows:

DW 1. “না জমিতে একটি খাল, একটি খানকয়ে চিশতিয়া ও কিছু বস্তি আছে।

DW 2. আমরা না জায়গায় দখলে যেতে পারিনি-নালিশী ১১৭ ও ১১৮ নং প্লট বিক্রি করেছে। কোম্পানী এর নিকট, তারা সেই জায়গায় দখল নিয়ে বিল্ডিং করেছে।

সরকার নাঃ জায়গায় ম্যানপাওয়ার ডিপাটংমেন্টে এর বিল্ডিং করেছে।”

19. We therefore, agree with Mr. Huq that no decree for mesne profits can be passed on these evidence even if we concede that the instant suit was maintainable. The suit suffers from vagueness as to the evidence on record.

This appeal is, therefore, dismissed without costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Civil Revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and order dated 25-10-93 passed by Mr. Md. Mohshin Mollah, Senior Assistant Judge, District Kishoreganj in OC Execution Case No. 4 of 1993 rejecting the application dated 2-9-1993 of the Judgment-debtor for dismissing the Execution case which arises out of OC Suit No. 105 of 1979 of the said Court.

2. Short facts involved in the case is, that the predecessors of opposite party Nos. 1(a)-(f) as plaintiffs filed OC Suit No. 105 of 1979 in the First Court of Munsif, Kishoreganj against the petitioner and the predecessors of these opposite party Nos. 2 (a)-2(f), 2 and 3 for ejectment of tenant.

3. The petitioner and the opposite party No. 3 filed written statement and contested the suit.

4. The suit of the plaintiff was decreed wherein the judgment was passed on 25-5-81 and the decree was signed on 3-6-1981. Against the aforesaid decree the tenant preferred OC Appeal No. 141 of 1981 before the learned District Judge Mymensingh who by his judgment dated 26-9-88 and decree dated 29-9-88 set aside the trial Court's aforesaid decree and thereafter the landlord filed Civil Revision No. 949 of 1988 before the High Court Division and the High Court Division by its judgment dated 17-2-93 set aside the appellate decree and restored that of the trial Court and that against the High Court Judgment the tenant preferred a review petition which was rejected by the High Court Division on 26-5-93 and Leave Petition No. 282 of 1993 was filed before the Appellate Division against the High Court Judgment by the tenant but the same was rejected by the Appellate Division on 2-9-93 and in the meanwhile the landlord (plaintiff) filed Execution Case No. 4 of 1993 on 10-4-1993; and thereafter on 2-9-93 the tenant filed an application in the aforesaid execution case for dismissal of the execution case on ground of limitation and the said application was rejected by the Executing Court by an order dated 25-10-93 and against this order the present revisional application has been filed by the petitioner and the petitioner obtained the Rule on 9-1-94.

5. Mr. AA Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that the judgment and order dated 25-10-93 is bad in law, arbitrary, unwarranted, illegal and liable to be set aside. Mr. Chowdhury has further submitted that the learned Court below failed to consider the question of limitation and thus came to an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Chowdhury had further submitted that the judgment being passed on 25-5-1981 and the decree being signed on 3-6-81 arising out of which the Execution Case in question was filed on 10-4-93 and the Execution case was barred under Article 181 of the Limitation Act, but the learned trial Court without considering this point of limitation was very much pleased to refer to one unrelated decision and came to an erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Chowdhury further submitted that the Execution Case in question should have been dismissed and in not doing so, the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law occasioning a failure of justice.

<u>6. Mr. Chowdhury in support of his contention has referred to 1 PLR 215 and has submitted that "limitation for an application to execute the decree or order runs from the date of decree or order sought to be executed". Mr. Chowdhury appearing for the petitioner then referred to 36 DLR (AD) 5 and has submitted that Article 182 requires that first application for execution is to be made within 3 years of the decree.</u>

7. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(f), has filed an affidavit in-opposition on behalf of the opposite party Nos. 1(a) to 1(1) and has stated that the petitioner intentionally did not state the facts that the present opposite parties predecessor filed OC Suit 105 of 1979 for ejectment of the monthly tenant (the present petitioner) from a shop on ground of bonafide requirement. Mr. Bhuiyan has given the dates of the trial Court's judgment and decree and the date of the appellate Court's judgment and the date of the judgment passed in the connected Civil Revision restoring that of the trial Court's judgment and decree and lastly, the date of judgment rejecting the leave petition of the tenant. Mr. Bhuiyan has submitted that in this case there was a continuation of proceeding and though the trial Court's judgment was made on 25-5-81 and the decree was signed on 3-6-81 and thereafter by the judgment of the appellate Court the decree of the trial Court was set aside and the decree of the landlord was a non entity till it was restored in the Civil Revision on 17-2-93 and the plaintiff (the landlord) could not file execution case to execute the decree which was a non entity till 17 -2-93 and in such view of the matter the landlord (the plaintiff) is in time in filing the execution case.

8. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has submitted that after the judgment of High Court Division dated 17 - 2-93 restoring the judgment of the trial Court the filing of the execution case on 10-4-93 is within time. in view of the provisions of Article 182 of the Limitation Act and. as a matter of fact. Article 182 of the Limitation Act is applicable in the instant case and Mr. Bhuiyan submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case the decision reported in 36 DLR (AD) 5 does not apply as the facts of the two cases are different

<u>9. Mr. Bhuiyan has referred to 12 DLR 730 and has submitted that an appeal includes revision and limitation runs from the order in revision under clause 2 of Article 82 of the Limitation Act.</u>

<u>10. Mr. Bhuiyan then referred to 33 DLR AD 101 and has submitted that a right to apply accrues on the final decree of the appellate Court or the revisional Court as the case may be (with effect from the date of the final (Decree) and in view of Article 182 of the Limitation Act. time should run from the date of the final decree and Mr. Bhuiyan referred to Article 182 of the Limitation Act which runs as follows:</u>

<u>Description of application</u>

<u>182: For the execution of a decree or order of any civil Court other than, (1) applications to which section 48 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, applies; and (2) applications provided for by Article 183.</u>

<u>Period of Limitation</u>

<u>Three years or, where a certified copy of the decree or order has been registered, six years.</u>

<u>Time from which period appealed from</u>

<u>1. The date of the decree or order, or</u>

<u>2. (Where there has been an appeal) the date of the final decree or order of the appellate Court, or the withdrawal of the appeal, or</u>

<u>3. (Where there has been a review of judgment) the date of the decision passed on the review, or</u>

<u>4. (Where the decree has been amended) the date of amendment, or</u>

<u>5. (Where the application next hereinafter mentioned has been made) the date of 1 (the final order passed on an application made) in accordance with law to the proper Court for execution or to take some step in aid of execution of the decree or order, or</u>

<u>6. (in respect of any amount, recovered by execution of the decree or order which the decree holder has been directed to refund by a decree passed in a suit for such refund) the date of such last mentioned decree. Or (in the case of an appeal therefrom) the date of the final decree of the Appellate Court or of the withdrawal of the appeal, or</u>

<u>7. (Where the application is to enforce any payment which the decree or order directs to be made at a certain date) such date.</u>

11. From the reading of sub-clauses 2, 3 and 6 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act I feel that time should run from the date of the final decree or order of the appellate Court or from the date of the decision passed on revision or review and from the date of such last mentioned decree or in the case of an appeal from the date of the final decree of the appellate Court. I think sub-clauses 2, 3 and 6 of Article 182 of the Limitation Act should be read together and there is no difficulty to say that the time should run from the date of the final decree and the right to apply for execution accrues on the date of the final decree of the appellate Court or Revisional Court.

12. In view of the discussions made above I find that the Court below committed no error of law in rejecting the application of the petitioner and I find no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order.

In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff- petitioner is against judgment and order dated 30.11.88 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Satkhira in Miscellaneous Case No. 79 of 1986.

2. Petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 51 of 1970 which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 514 of 1981 for declaration of title in the suit land measuring 11.64 acres. The said suit was contested amongst others, by defendant No.15 by filing written statement. In the said written statement defendant No.15 disclosed that he sold some of the suit lands to opposite party and others. Thereafter the plaintiff impleaded those purchasers as defendant Nos. 30-36. The suit was ultimately decreed ex parte on 21.8.85. Being aggrieved by the same opposite party who was defendant No. 36 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 79 of 1986 of 31.7.85 alleging that summons and registered post card of the suit were not served upon him and he came to know about the said ex parte decree on 29.7.86. Petitioner contested the said Miscellaneous case denying the material allegations and asserting that summons and registered post card were duly served upon the said defendant and he did not contest the suit as he would get no relief in the suit and story of his knowledge from one Binoy Krishna on 27.7.86 is not correct and manufactured.

3. After considering the evidence the Court below allowed the case by the impugned judgment. Being aggrieved by the same petitioner obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr. Syed Golam Mostafa, appearing for the petitioner, submitted that from order No. 88 dated 26.2.76 recording service of summons upon the defendant Nos.30-36 and order No. 89 dated 25.3.76 recording appearance of defendant Nos. 30-36 and filing of separate applications by them adopting written statement filed by the defendant No.15 it is clear that opposite party had knowledge of the suit from 25.3.76. He also submitted that opposite party having not denied filing of vokalatnama and application on 25.3.76 adopting written statement of defendant No. 15 either in his application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC or in his deposition as PW 1 the Court below was not justified in not relying upon the Court's orders recording service of summons and appearance of defendant No.36 merely because the return of the summons and the vokalatnama were missing from the record and in comparing signature of the said defendant appearing in the said application with his other admitted signatures.

5. It appears from the impugned judgment that Court below on consideration of evidence of the PWs and OPWs and also order No. 88 dated 26.2.76 concluded that the petitioner failed to prove that summons were served upon the said defendant No. 36. It further appears that Court below compared purported signatures of defendant No. 36 appearing in application dated 25.3.76 with his admitted signatures in the application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC, vokalatnama filed therewith and his deposition as PW 1, and concluded that it has not been proved that the said signatures appearing in the said application is that of the defendant No.36. It further appears that Court below found that the case was not barred by limitation.

6. It appears from paragraph 3 of the application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC filed by the opposite party that he came to know about the said ex parte decree on 27.7.86 from PW 2 Binoy Krishna and then he made enquiry from the Court below on 29.7.86 and came to know the details about the said suit. It appears that he filed the said Miscellaneous Case on 31.7.86. It is curious to note that though the opposite party came to know details about the suit after making enquiry from the Court below on 29.7.86 he has not denied that he appeared in the suit on 25.3.76 by filing vokalatnama and filed an application on that date adopting written statement of defendant No. 15. Even in his deposition opposite party did not deny his signature appearing in the said application dated 25.3.76 adopting written statement filed by defendant No. 15. But the fact remains that the return of the summons served upon defendant Nos. 32 to 36 and the vokalatnama filed by them on 25.3.76 are missing from the record. Though Court below noticed missing of these two important documents having serious bearing upon the decision of the case it failed to draw the necessary inference in the matter. It was none of the business of the Court below to compare signature of defendant No.36 appearing in the application dated 25.3.76 with his admitted signatures when that very signature was not denied in the application under Order 9 rule 13 CPC or in the deposition of opposite party as PW 1. On comparison of the signatures from the LC Records at the time of hearing of the Rule it appears that there is similarity in the said signatures.

<u>7. It may be noted that defendant No. 13 filed a written statement in the suit disclosing that he sold some of the suit property to the opposite party and others and thereafter defendant Nos. 30-36 including the opposite party were impleaded in the suit. Though defendant No. 15 asserted in his written statement that plaintiff petitioner has no title and possession of the suit property he did not ultimately contest the suit. It is not unnatural on the part of the opposite party who derived interest from defendant No. 15 that he would adopt written statement filed by his vendor. He having not challenged the filing of the said application reason for missing of his vokalatnama and service return of summons on him is not far to seek. When the opposite party did not challenge the filing of power and application on 25.3.76 from order No. 89 dated 25.3.76 recording the same, it could be safely inferred that he was aware of the suit at least from that date. Court below was not justified in not relying upon the same on an erroneous finding that the signature of defendant No. 36 appearing in the said application was not proved overlooking that the same was not even challenged. Men may lie but circumstances cannot. Circumstances noticed above clearly show that the opposite party had knowledge of the suit at least from 25.3.76 and he filed that case with allegations which were belied by the unchallenged record of the case. So oral testimony contrary to the aforesaid orders recorded by the Court in due course of business cannot be relied on unless it could be shown that the same were obtained by practising fraud upon the Court In such circumstances the finding of the Court below that the summons were not served upon the opposite party and he was not aware of the suit and ex parte decree before 27.7.86 cannot be sustained in law and, as such, impugned judgment suffers from error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.</u>

In the result, the Rule is made absolute without cost and the impugned judgment and order setting aside the ex parte decree and restoring the suit is set aside.

End.

full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.: This leave petition by the writ petitioner is from the judgment and order of the High Court Division discharging the Rule Nisi, in Writ Petition No. 1677 of 1988.

2. Claiming that the house property at 2/11 Block 'A', Sir Syed Ahmed Road, PS Mohammadpur, Dhaka was the subject matter of an agreement of sale on 7.1.71 between Dr. Sadrul Hasan, the then owner thereof and the petitioner and further claiming that the petitioner obtained an ex parte decree on 11.4.83 in a suit for specific performance of contract, namely, Title Suit No. 1441 of 1981 from the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the said Dr. Sadrul Hasan and that the petitioner obtained a deed of sale through Court in execution thereof, the petitioner challenged the inclusion of the said property in list, 'Ka' under section 5(1)(a) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 before the Court of Settlement, respondent No. 1, in Case No 794 of 1987.

3. Respondent, No. 1 by its judgment dated 6.8.88 accepted the contention of the respondent-Government that Dr. Sadrul Hasan was not present in this country both during and after the liberation of the country, that the property was declared as an abandoned property, that the Government possessed it through its allottees, that the alleged agreement dated 7.1.71 is an ante-dated agreement and that the petitioner obtained an ex parte decree in respect of an abandoned property which is in executable.

4. The High Court Division being moved against the said judgment discharged the Rule Nisi upon agreeing with respondent No. 1 in its material findings and further holding that the suit of the petitioner was barred by limitation under Article 113 of the Limitation Act.

5. Mr. Moksumul Hakim, learned Counsel for the petitioner, submits that it was not taken into consideration that the Government-defendant filed Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1985 under Order 9, rule 13, CPC against the ex parte decree dated 11.4.83 which was pending on the date of publication of the petitioner's property in the 'Ka' list. He submits that the proviso (b) to section 5(1) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 provides that no such list shall include any building in respect of which, inter alia, an application was pending before any Court.

6. The submission has no substance. The suit, appeal or application pending on the date of publication must be of a stated type. Mr. Hakim failed to show that either the suit or the misc. case answered the description given in the said proviso.

7. Mr. Hakim submits next that the High Court Division failed to consider that if the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case No. 16 of 1985 is disposed of either way, there will be possibility of conflict between a decree of a civil Court and a judgment of the Court of Settlement.

8. This submission is devoid of substance. The Court of Settlement has held that the building is an abandoned property, that it has vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 1972 and that the petitioner has no right or interest in the building. The High Court Division has confirmed this finding. The ex parte decree and the miscellaneous case are valueless under the circumstances.

9. Mr. Hakim next submits that the Court of Settlement disposed of the matter in a summary way and its conclusions are far from satisfactory, which the High Court Division failed to notice.

<u>10. So long as the Court of Settlement acts within jurisdiction and does not commit any excess of jurisdiction the High Court Division will be right in not interfering on the ground of mere unsatisfactory disposal of a case.</u>

11. Mr. Hakim then draws our attention to clause 2 of the agreement dated 7.1.71 between Dr. Sadrul Hasan and the petitioner and submits that the vendor had time upto 7.1.81 to execute and register the deed of sale and the petitioner had time upto 7.1.84 to file the suit She filed the suit on 14.12.81 Hence the suit was not barred by limitation.

12. This argument is not available to the petitioner as neither either plaint of the suit nor the agreement was produced before the Court of Settlement or before the High Court Division.

13. No other ground or point has been urged by Mr. Hakim.

The petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani J: This Rule is directed against the order passed in a Miscellaneous Case under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure allowing amendment of its original application.

2. The facts and circumstances leading to this Rule are as follows: The petitioners before us instituted a title suit for declaration of their certain share in the compensation money for acquisition of the lands in schedule; 'A' and for partition of land in schedule 'B'. There were 118 defendants. Third, fourth and fifth defendants contested the suit jointly by filing a written statement, but the contest ended in compromise. Consequently the suit was decreed in terms of solenama as against defendant Nos. 3-5 and ex parte against the rest. Subsequently final decree for partition was put into execution and on the basis of the report of the advocate commissioner the parties to the solenam a including the petitioners got the lands alloted in their respective saham. Afterwards three among the non-contesting defendants filed a miscellaneous case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for selling aside both the preliminary and final decrees for partition. Ultimately this case was allowed, ex parte decrees were set aside and the suit was restored to its original file and number. Thereafter those defendants filed Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1992 under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restoration of possession of the decretal properties. The case is pending. The petitioners in the said case filed an application under Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of their original application. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed the application for amendment by the order dated 17.4.93 and against thereof the petitioners obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, submits that an application under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure being not a pleading the provisions of rule 17 of Order 6 is not attracted and the Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in entertaining the application for amendment of the pleading in the said case.

<u>4. The point raised by Mr. Alam is required to be recast elaborately for proper consideration, that is to say, whether a case under section 144, CPC is a proceedings as mentioned in section 141, CPC so that the procedure provided in the Code in regard to suits like that for amendment (Order 6 rule 17) can be made applicable in the instant case.</u>

<u>5. The answer to this question is that the proceedings mentioned in section 141 obviously refer to original cases in the nature of suits, such as probate case, guardianship case and the like and not the other cases which do not originate in themselves, but arise out of a suit or some other proceedings, We agree with the observation made in 5 DLR 269 by a learned Single Judge that effect of section 141 is that procedure in regard to suit can be extended only to proceedings of original nature. Keeping this in view, it is not difficult to say that a proceeding under section 144 is not an original case wherein procedure in regard to suits as contained in CPC can be made applicable.</u>

6. Majority view in AIR 1965 (SC) 1477 is that an application for restitution under section 144 is an application for execution of a decree. In 17 All 106 (PC) their Lordships in the Privy Council held that section 141 does not apply to applications for execution.

7. We, therefore, find that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the impugned decision in allowing the aforesaid application for amendment of the original application of the miscellaneous case under section 144 CPC.

8. The result is that this Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned order elated 17.4.93 passed by the Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case No. 30 of 1990 is set aside and the application [or amendment dated 18.3.93 is rejected.

The learned Advocate for the opposite parties submits that this Court while disposing of Civil Revision No. 386 of 1990 directed the learned Subordinate Judge to dispose of the original suit within 6(six) months of the receipt of its order dated 17.7.92. It appears that the order had not been complied with and the learned Subordinate Judge is once again directed to dispose of the suit within 6 (six) months from the date of receipt of this order.

End.

Fazle Munim, J.: This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Second Miscellaneous Appeal No. 9 of 1973 on July 30, 1979.

2. The respondent filed a case before the Chairman, Kalibari Union Committee, Barisal against the appellant and another for arrears of house rent and obtained a decree. The decree was put into execution in the Second Court of Munsif of Barisal. The appellant who was the judgment debtor instituted an objection under section 47 CPC being Miscellaneous case No. 48 of 1970, in the same Court for a declaration that the decree obtained by the respondent was illegal and without jurisdiction since there is no written contract of monthly tenancy. Further, he asserted that there was no relationship of landlord and tenant between him and the respondent and that he was in possession of the property in his own right. The said case was allowed by the Munsif. Respondent preferred an appeal, being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 19 of 1972, before the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal who allowed the appeal and restored the execution case. Being aggrieved, the Appellant filed the aforesaid Second Miscellaneous Appeal before the High Court Division which upheld the judgment of the first appellate Court. Against the decision of the High Court Division the appellant moved this Court and obtained leave to appeal on the following grounds:

i) Whether the conciliation Court has the jurisdiction to decide the claim in the absence of written contract.

ii) Whether Part II(b), which gives jurisdiction, speaks about the 'contract receipts' or 'other' documents and whether it shows that the contract must be written contract;

iii) Whether in absence of such written contract the jurisdiction of the conciliation Court is not attracted."

3. Mr. SS Halder, Counsel for the appellant, contended that the conciliation Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the case filed by the respondent as there was no written contract of monthly tenancy. In support of his contention he placed reliance on a decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court, namely, Zamiruddin Vs. Havas Khan 21 DLR (SC) 39. The provisions of law conferring jurisdiction on the conciliation Court are contained in Part 1 (b) of the Conciliation Courts Ordinance (XLIV of 1961).

4. In interpreting whether the word 'contract' as occurs in sub-section 1 of Section B Part I of the schedule which confers jurisdiction in respect of "suit for the recovery of money due on contract, receipts or order documents" on the Union Council if the impugned claim does not exceed Taka 500.00, is an oral contract or written contract the Supreme Court of Pakistan observed as follows:

“The learned counsel for the appellant has drawn our attention to two decisions of the East Pakistan High Court wherein suits based on oral contracts were found to be exclusively triable by Conciliation Courts. These decisions arc reported as Muhammad Nurul Islam alias Nurul Vs. Anath Ram Sarma 17 DLR 261 and Civil Reference No. 1 of 17 DLR 415. We may point out that in these cases the question whether the word "contracts" in sub-section 1 of section B of Part I of the schedule includes both oral and written contracts was not specifically raised. In our view, the context in which the word contracts have been used in the said provision clearly indicates that written contracts are only meant."

<u>5. We respectfully differ with the above interpretation of the word 'contract' as given by the Supreme Court of Pakistan. No reason is available as to why the word 'contract' should not include an oral contract. For deciding this question, we may refer to the Contract Act. In the Contract Act any agreement which is enforceable by law is a contract. The Act nowhere says that an oral agreement is not enforceable by law, or that a written agreement only is enforceable by law. The word 'contract' may, therefore, mean either an oral or a written contract. In the Conciliation Court Ordinance the word 'contract' has not been qualified in any way, in particular, whether this is to mean and include only a written contract. In this context, it must, therefore, be held that the word 'contract' should embrace an oral contract as well as a written one.</u>

6. In this view of the matter we find no reason to say that the conciliation Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the respondent's case based on an oral contract of monthly tenancy.

The appeal is, therefore, dismissed with costs.

End.
